text: ## **Transport – Aviation** The aviation sector includes customers that are commercial airline operators that offer scheduled services, and aircraft lessors to such operators.[ 3] Where CBA had less than $5 million of TCE to a customer at the reporting date, the customer was excluded from the scope of the goal in order to focus data collection efforts on more material exposures. For aviation the goal metric is an intensity metric (gCO2/revenue passenger km) calculated by dividing attributed ‘tank-to-wake’ emissions[ 4] (Scope 1 for operators and Scope 33 for lessors), in gCO2, by attributed revenue passenger kilometres (RPK). This reflects the continued role of aviation in a decarbonising world. We source emissions and RPK data from airline sustainability reporting for exposures to airlines or lessors where the lessee is known. Where data is not available, including for lessors where the lessees are unknown, emissions intensity is estimated using the portfolio average. Where CO2 data is unavailable, we use CO2-e. However, we include Scope 2 (Scope 3 ‘indirect electricity’ for lessors) absolute emissions for this sector, which are generally minimal, within our financed emissions disclosure. Attribution follows the PCAF business lending methodology. For lessors where the lessee is known, the attribution factor denominator is the total equity and debt or EVIC of the lessee and the attribution factor numerator is drawn lending exposure to the lessee. As lending in our aviation portfolio generally relates to specific aircraft within an airline’s fleet, we may seek to improve the accuracy of our financed emissions estimates for this sector over time by substituting airline level data with aircraft specific data and adapting our attribution approach accordingly.

## **Transport – Shipping** The shipping sector includes customers that operate ocean-going vessels, and ocean-going vessel lessors to such operators.¹ Where CBA had less than $5 million of TCE to a customer at the reporting date, the customer was excluded from the scope of the target to focus data collection efforts on more material exposures. For shipping the target metric is absolute financed emissions, calculated based on attributed ‘tank-to-wake’ emissions[ 2] (Scope 1 for operators and Scope 3[ 1] lessors), in MtCO2. Where CO2 data is unavailable, we use CO2-e. We have selected an absolute emissions metric for this interim target due to data limitations. For exposures to shipping companies, we source emissions data from customers’ sustainability reporting. For lessors, where the lessee is known we source emissions data from the lessee’s sustainability reporting. Where data is not available, including for lessees, emissions are estimated using the average emissions intensity per dollar of drawn lending for customers with available emissions data. Our sector-level financed emissions target for shipping is a Scope 1 (Scope 3 ‘tank-to-wake’ for lessors) target, to align to the scope of the reference scenario. However, we include Scope 2 (Scope 3 ‘indirect electricity’ for lessors) absolute emissions for this sector, which are generally minimal, within our financed emissions disclosure. Attribution follows the PCAF business lending methodology. For lessors where the lessee is known, the attribution factor denominator is the total equity and debt or EVIC of the lessee and the attribution factor numerator is drawn lending exposure to the lessee. We track the portfolio emissions against the IEA NZE (2021) global pathway for shipping. A global reference scenario is appropriate given the global nature of our portfolio.

## **Heavy industry – Steel** The steel sector includes production of steel with iron and steel mills. For steel, the alignment metric is tCO2-e/tonne steel production. An intensity metric reflects the role of metals production in a decarbonising world. This goal has been set without a baseline as there were no customers with drawn lending at the time the goal was set. Our sector-level financed emissions goal for steel is a Scope 1 and 2 intensity goal, to align to the scope of the reference scenario. There were no customers with drawn exposure in this sector as at 30 June 2022, 30 June 2023 or 30 June 2024. If there were, we would include Scope 3 absolute emissions for such customers within the heavy industry sector presented in our financed emissions disclosure. The selected reference scenario is from the SBTi Steel target-setting tool (consultation draft, version 2.2), using an emissions intensity of 1.91 tCO2/tonne steel for the base year of 2021, sourced from the World Steel Association.[ 3] The scrap ratio numbers used in the tool are sourced from the IEA with 31% for the base year and 37% in the goal year (2030).[ 4]

## **Heavy industry – Alumina and aluminium** The alumina and aluminium sector includes the refining of bauxite to form alumina and the smelting of alumina to produce aluminium. This excludes secondary production such as aluminium recycling. For both alumina and aluminium, the alignment metric is tCO2-e/tonne aluminium production. This follows industry convention in expressing alumina production in terms of aluminium equivalents. We use the industry-accepted factor of 1.9 tonnes alumina production per 1.0 tonne of aluminium for this conversion. An intensity metric reflects the role of metals production in a decarbonising world. For Scope 1 and 2, where a company does not report emissions for alumina and aluminium separately, we estimate emissions to alumina and aluminium by applying a location-specific emissions factor for alumina emissions intensity and aluminium emissions intensity to available data on the customer’s refining and smelting production activity, respectively. Our sector-level financed emissions goals for alumina and aluminium are Scope 1 and 2 intensity goals, to align to the scope of the reference scenario. However, we include Scope 3 absolute emissions for these customers within the heavy industry sector presented in our financed emissions disclosure. Where a customer does not report Scope 3 emissions these are estimated by multiplying the customer’s reported Scope 1 and 2 emissions by a Scope 3 emissions factor. The Scope 3 emissions factor represents the ratio of Scope 1 and 2 emissions to Scope 3 emissions for the portfolio of customers in the alumina and aluminium sector for which we have a complete set of reported Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions. The selected reference scenarios are the MPP Oceania 1.5°C alumina and aluminium pathways. We track the portfolio emissions intensity against the IEA NZE (2021) global pathway for aviation. A global reference scenario is appropriate given the global nature of our portfolio. > 1 Motor vehicle finance includes commercial asset finance and consumer personal loans. Legacy Bankwest personal loans are excluded due to data limitations. > 2 Note that emissions by vehicle type are reported by BITRE on a CO2-e basis. ## **Heavy industry – Cement** The cement sector includes manufacturing portland, natural and other hydraulic cement from crushed limestone and clay or shale. For cement, the alignment metric is tCO2-e/tonne cement production. An intensity metric reflects the role of cement production in buildings and construction. We define cement as cementitious product, which aligns with the GHG Protocol’s ‘specific CO2 per ton of cementitious product’ definition. This means that our sector-level financed emissions goal for cement is a Scope 1 and Scope 2 intensity goal. This aligns with the boundary of the reference scenario used for the goal. Emissions and production associated with imported clinker and clinker purchased from third parties (typically reported as Scope 3) are not included in the goal. However, we include Scope 3 absolute emissions for cement sector customers within the heavy industry sector presented in our financed emissions disclosure. The selected reference scenario is from the SBTi Cement target-setting tool (Version 2.1.2), using an emissions intensity of 0.708 tCO2-e Scope 1 emissions/tonnes of cement, for the base year of 2021, sourced from the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW).[ 1] While this baseline and resulting sector-level pathway only accounts for Scope 1 emissions, we adopt a conservative approach by comparing it against our annual intensity metric which is inclusive of both Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions.

## **Upstream oil and gas extraction** Upstream oil extraction refers to entities whose principal operations include the exploration and development of oil fields for the purposes of extracting and producing crude oil. This does not include midstream or downstream activities. Upstream gas extraction refers to entities whose principal operations include exploration, ownership, development and management of gas fields, that are used for the purpose of natural gas production. For upstream oil and gas extraction the target metric is absolute emissions. Where a customer reports emissions, we assign emissions to upstream oil and gas extraction using a ‘pro-rata’ share based on the customer’s production of oil and gas and the emissions factor for each activity, respectively, expressed in ‘million barrels of oil equivalent’. Where customer-level emissions data is not available, the customer’s reported production data is multiplied by an activity emissions intensity factor[ 2] to estimate Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions. Scope 3 emissions are estimated by first converting production, in barrels of oil equivalent, to energy content using an energy content factor from third-party sources such as Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy and then multiplying the energy content by emissions factors from the National Greenhouse Accounts. We calculate our upstream oil and gas extraction targets using the percentage decrease of emissions from combustion activities, oil and natural gas respectively between 2020 and 2030 from the IEA NZE (2021) scenario.

## **Thermal coal mining** The thermal coal mining sector includes companies that mine thermal coal. We include all thermal coal mining customers with more than 5% of their revenue coming directly from the sale of thermal coal in our 2030 target. For thermal coal mining the target metric is absolute emissions. Where customer-level emissions data is not available, the customer’s reported production data is multiplied by a physical emissions intensity factor[ 2] to estimate Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions. Scope 3 emissions are estimated by multiplying production by National Greenhouse Accounts energy content and emissions factors for bituminous coal. Where a customer reports coal emissions, we assign emissions to thermal coal mining using a ‘pro-rata’ share based on the customer’s production of thermal coal as a proportion of total coal: coal emissions x (thermal coal production/total coal production). We calculate our thermal coal mining target using the percentage decrease of emissions from coal combustion activities between 2020 and 2030 from the IEA NZE (2021) scenario. Our E&S Framework details our commitments regarding thermal coal mining financing. We have set a 2030 interim target for thermal coal mining, to reduce our financed emissions in thermal coal mining by 100% from our 2020 baseline. This represents a faster reduction than the IEA NZE (2021) scenario.

Approach to climate scenario analysis**

## **Long-term scenarios and CRMA** Climate scenario analysis is a rapidly evolving field, with global scenarios regularly produced and updated. We use assumptions and inputs drawing from credible, global climate scenarios produced by the NGFS and obtain input from external experts when necessary. We review our choice of scenarios to check, in our view, they have plausible and appropriately severe outcomes; are consistent with legislative requirements and market practices, including use by peer banks; and they have appropriate sector and geographic data readily available. We use a combination of credible, long-term global climate scenarios that provide consistent inputs and assumptions for differing futures, as well as a range of acute scenarios to explore the impact of individual severe physical and transition events that could impact the Bank in any given year. This approach helps us to consider the changing impacts on the Bank’s financial prospects and risk profile over time, due to long-term chronic physical risks; increasingly frequent and severe acute physical risks; evolving transition risks arising from regulatory change, technological advancements and evolving stakeholder expectations; and opportunities that may arise to improve climate resilience and finance the transition. Depending on the nature of changes in the scenarios, in some cases, we may look to rerun previous analyses using updated information.

There are a range of uncertainties when looking to model scenarios and their climate-related impacts. Understanding uncertainty within climate modelling allows us to focus on reducing it where possible, accepting it where necessary, and interpreting and communicating results in an appropriate manner. We consider the risks of relying on uncertain information when making decisions based on climate scenario analysis and we aim to avoid false precision in modelled outcomes, for example by rating physical risk across an entire portfolio rather than expecting single address results to be equally robust. There are limitations and uncertainties associated with projections of future climate scenarios, given the limitations of current scientific understanding of the climate system, its cascading impact to the broader economy and society, and complexity of climate risk modelling. The table below highlights a non-exhaustive list of some of the key sources of uncertainty and the range of limitations. - **Modelling area Key sources of uncertainty and limitations Long-term** • Global climate models are highly complex and can be used to simulate possible future climates under **climate scenarios** various scenarios, such as different global warming trends. While they are grounded in physical principles and evaluated against past observations, their projections carry uncertainty due to the complexity of the climate system. - Economic variables for long-term scenarios are projected over a 25-year time horizon, with assumptions regarding factors such as policy and technology. There is considerable uncertainty over the pace and impact of climate change on the environment (physical risk) as well as how global and domestic governments will act to address it (transition risk). These projections could therefore be inaccurate. - Long-term scenarios do not attempt to predict the timing and extent of individual acute physical or transition events that could materially impact the Bank’s financial performance in any given year. Rather, the cumulative effect of such events is factored into macroeconomic variables used to model these trends. Although this approach enables a clearer view of any trends over time, it underestimates potential losses to the Bank because it does not account for localised declines, or direct impacts on asset values from severe climate physical or transition events that could occur in any given year. - Climate transition risk can materialise in a variety of ways including through direct exposure to carbon prices or indirect impacts from reduced demand. Our portfolio exposure to physical and transition risks** Our assessment of the Bank’s financial exposure to climate risk considers the extent to which regions or industries we lend to are currently exposed to elevated physical and/or transition risks. On page 144 we have analysed sub-sectors of our Group TCE that may be exposed to elevated climate-related physical or transition risk. The footnotes below outline our key judgements, assumptions, inclusions and exclusions in the presentation of the table on page 144. 1. During the year we have revised the scope of our consumer portfolio to include Unloan home loans. Comparative information has been restated to conform to presentation in the current period. 2. Excluding consumer, sub-sectors are primarily based on a customer’s ANZSIC classification. Where this does not provide the granularity required, additional classification is undertaken using business knowledge. Our total sector exposures represent the Group including ASB. 3. Identification of physical risk in Australian home loans was based on modelled loss rates (cyclone, flood and fire), property location and topography (sea-level rise). The Bank applies a physical risk score based on the estimated risk of a hazard to the property. For example, properties are characterised as having a ‘high’ flood risk if they are located within an approximately 1-in-50-year flood zone. 4. Identification of high transition risk in Australian home loans was based on where local economies are assessed as heavily reliant on the fossil fuel value chain. For the non-consumer portfolio, high transition risk identification is performed at the sub-sector, or grouped ANZSIC level, based on greater impact from policy, technology and market changes under the transition to a lower-carbon economy. This framework was developed based on United Nations Environment Programme Finance Initiative’s industry guidance. 5. Of the consumer portfolio, only Australian home loans, excluding HELs and HELOCs including VLOCs, were assessed for physical and transition risks. The assessed portfolio also excludes RMG. A number of exposures were exposed to multiple risks however are summarised independently in this report. The totals do not reflect double counting in these exposures. 6. text: ## **Environmental management systems and certifications** We measure and manage the environmental impacts of our activities under our operational control using an environmental management system. Envizi is the platform used for Australia, India and our other overseas locations to manage environmental data and measure operational emissions. For New Zealand, ASB measures its operational emissions using in-house emissions calculators.

## **Certifications** - ISO 9001:2015 – Quality Management System. Scope of certification: the Management of delivery of retail capital works incorporating sustainability and digital engineering aspects. - ISO 14001:2015 – Environmental Management System. Scope of certification: the provision of property operations and facilities management across Australian operations for the Group, including commercial office spaces, retail banking branches, data centres, SST (ATMs). - ISO 50001:2018 – Energy Management System. Scope of certification: the provision of property operations and facilities management across Australian operations for the Group including commercial office spaces, retail banking branches, data centres, SST (ATMs).

## **Operational emissions targets** Our operational emissions targets publicly document the measurement, target setting and our progress to reduce emissions over time. We set our targets in conjunction with an environmental consultant and periodically review to ensure they remain representative of the Bank’s operations; however, we do not currently have our targets validated by a third party. Our external auditor provides reasonable assurance for Scope 1 and 2 operational emissions and limited assurance for selected Scope 3 operational emissions over point-in-time performance and we report these against the targets. Our operational targets are gross absolute emissions reductions, with carbon offsets not included in progress tracking. **Scope 1 and 2 operational emissions reduction target:** This target is based on a 1.5˚C trajectory. Emissions relate to the consumption of natural gas, stationary fuel, refrigerant and electricity used in retail, commercial and data centre properties under the Group’s operational control, and business use of tool-of-trade vehicles. Market-based reporting is used to reflect the impact of sourcing electricity needs from renewable sources. Electricity emissions are reported where we are unable to purchase renewable electricity due to data limitations. **Scope 3 operational emissions reduction target:** This target encompasses selected Scope 3 emissions sources and is based on a 1.5˚C trajectory, excluding flights, which is based on a well-below 2˚C trajectory. To ensure the baseline is representative of a typical year, Scope 3 business travel emissions are adjusted to FY19 values to normalise for the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. Includes indirect greenhouse gas emissions as a result of sources outside the Group’s operational control, but support the Group’s business activities. Base building, business use of private vehicles and work from home emissions are excluded. Due to data limitations, New Zealand emissions exclude upstream stationary and transport fuels, and freight emissions. Only flight emissions are included for limited other overseas operations due to data limitations at the time of target setting.

## **Organisational boundaries** We set our organisational boundary and measure our operational emissions with reference to the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard, accounting for the operations, facilities and subsidiaries owned or controlled by the Group. We take an operational control approach to establish our boundary for reporting our operational emissions inventory. We have extended our boundary to include selected Scope 3 emissions sources beyond our operational control that occur as part of the Group’s value chain activities and where reliable data is available. **Australia:** Encompasses our Australia-based operations, including Bankwest, and includes commercial, retail and residential properties, data centres, ATMs and our company fleet. We have extended our boundary to include selected Scope 3 emissions sources beyond our operational control. **New Zealand:** Encompasses the subsidiaries, operations and facilities owned or controlled by ASB and includes our corporate offices, regional centres, data centres, branches and ATMs. We have extended our boundary to include selected Scope 3 emissions sources beyond our operational control. CBA New Zealand emissions for these categories have been assessed as not material. **India:** Includes our commercial office and operations in India. **Other overseas:** Represents Group operations and controlled entities outside Australia, New Zealand and India, and includes all other offices located in North America, Asia and Europe.

## **Calculating operational emissions** Group operational emissions for 2025 have been measured and prepared, in all material respects, with reference to the Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (revised edition) and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol: Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard (GHG Protocol). For Australia, India, and other overseas, invoices or reports are received from the relevant data source and are loaded into Envizi. The platform then calculates the emissions using the relevant emissions factors. Emissions factors are reviewed by a third party for CBA and updated in Envizi. For ASB in New Zealand, invoices or reports are received from the relevant data source and the relevant emissions factors are applied to calculate the emissions using in-house emissions calculators.

## **Scope 1 emissions** Scope 1 operational emissions are direct emissions from operations that are owned or controlled by the reporting company. This relates to the Group’s consumption of natural gas, stationary fuel and refrigerants used in retail, commercial and data centre properties under the Group’s operational control and business use of tool-of-trade vehicles, during the reporting period. The consumption data is based on a combination of invoiced amounts and estimates based on historical information or pro-rata consumption. ## **Scope 2 emissions** Scope 2 operational emissions are indirect emissions from the Group’s purchase of electricity used in retail, commercial, residential and data centre properties, SSTs (ATMs) and charging of the EV fleet under the Group’s operational control during the reporting period. The consumption data is based on a combination of invoiced amounts and estimates based on historical information or pro-rata consumption. Emissions are calculated using the relevant emissions factors noted in this section. This is the Criteria for the accompanying Selected Sustainability Information assured by PwC.

## **Selected Scope 3 emissions** Selected Scope 3 operational emissions are all other indirect emissions (not included in Scope 2) that occur in the value chain of the reporting company. This is the Criteria for the accompanying Selected Sustainability Information assured by PwC. The tables below outline all selected Scope 3 operational emissions sources and the emissions factors used to calculate emissions reported within our Annual Report. **For a reconciliation between Scope 3 operational emissions and those within our Scope 3 target, see page 428.** We use a location-based and market-based reporting approach. Location-based methodology reflects the average emissions intensity of grids on which energy consumption occurs, while a market-based methodology reflects emissions from electricity that we have purposefully chosen to purchase. text: ## **Responsibilities of Management** Management of the Group is responsible for the preparation of the Subject Matter Information in accordance with the Criteria. This responsibility includes: - determining appropriate reporting topics and selecting or establishing suitable criteria for measuring, evaluating and preparing the underlying Subject Matter Information; The Board of Directors of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia engaged us to perform independent reasonable and limited assurance, as applicable, in respect of selected Environmental, Social and Governance metrics and selected Sustainability Funding Target and Sector-level performance metrics (the Subject Matter Information) presented in the Commonwealth Bank of Australia 2025 Annual Report (the ‘2025 Annual Report’).

## **Subject Matter Information and Criteria** - ensuring that those criteria are relevant and appropriate to the Group and the intended users; and - designing, implementing and maintaining systems, processes and internal controls relevant to the preparation of the Subject Matter Information, which is free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, against the Criteria. The maintenance and integrity of the Group’s website is the responsibility of the Group’s management; the work carried out by us does not involve consideration of these matters and, accordingly, we accept no responsibility for any changes that may have occurred to the reported Subject Matter Information or Criteria when presented on the Group’s website. Specifically, we were engaged to assure the following subject matter information: - Limited Assurance over selected Sustainability Information (the Limited Assurance Sustainability Information), as outlined in Appendix 1 (i), - Reasonable Assurance over selected Sustainability Information (the Reasonable Assurance Sustainability Information), as outlined in Appendix 1 (ii), - Limited Assurance over selected Climate Subject Matter Information (the Limited Assurance Climate Information), as outlined in Appendix 1 (iii). together, the Subject Matter Information. The criteria used by the Group to prepare the selected Limited and Reasonable Assurance Sustainability Information is set out within the Climate disclosures appendix on pages 419 to 427 and the Glossary on pages 438 to 451 (‘the Sustainability Criteria’). Specifically, the Sustainability Criteria is identified within the Climate disclosures appendix and the Glossary by way of the following sentence: _This is the Criteria for the accompanying Selected Sustainability Information assured by PwC_ . We assessed the Limited and Reasonable Assurance Sustainability Information against the Sustainability Criteria. The Limited and Reasonable Assurance Sustainability Information needs to be read and understood together with the Sustainability Criteria, as at 30 June 2025 and the year/period then ended, or as otherwise specified in the Selected Sustainability Information set out on pages 95 to 99 and pages 167 to 169. The criteria used by the Group to prepare the selected Limited Assurance Climate Information is set out as follows (the Climate Criteria): 1. In the Sustainability Funding Target table presented on pages 416 to 418 of the 2025 Annual Report; and 2. In the Methodology presented on pages 392 to 405 as it relates to sector-level performance metrics and PCAF quality scores. The Sustainability Criteria and Climate Criteria are collectively referred to as ‘the Criteria’.

## **Our independence and quality management** We have complied with the ethical requirements of the Accounting Professional and Ethical Standard Board’s APES 110 _Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants (including Independence Standards)_ relevant to assurance engagements, which are founded on fundamental principles of integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality and professional behaviour. Our firm applies Australian Standard on Quality Management ASQM 1, _Quality Management for Firms that Perform Audits or Reviews of Financial Reports and Other Financial Information_ , or _Other Assurance or Related Services Engagements_ , which requires the firm to design, implement and operate a system of quality management including policies or procedures regarding compliance with ethical requirements, professional standards and applicable legal and regulatory requirements.

## **Limited Assurance Subject Matter Information** Our responsibility is to express a conclusion on the Limited Assurance Sustainability Information, as outlined in Appendix 1 (i), and the Limited Assurance Climate Information, as outlined in Appendix 1 (iii), based on the procedures we have performed and the evidence we have obtained. Our engagement has been conducted in accordance with the Australian Standard on Assurance Engagements (ASAE) 3000 _Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information and ASAE 3410 Assurance Engagements on Greenhouse Gas Statements_ . Those standards require that we plan and perform this engagement to obtain limited assurance about whether anything has come to our attention to indicate that the Limited Assurance Sustainability Information and Limited Assurance Climate Information, have not been prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the Criteria, for the years ended or periods as at, as outlined in Appendices 1 (i) and (iii). The procedures performed in a limited assurance engagement vary in nature and timing from, and are less in extent than for, a reasonable assurance engagement and consequently the level of assurance obtained in a limited assurance engagement is substantially lower than the assurance that would have been obtained had a reasonable assurance engagement been performed. Accordingly, we do not express a reasonable assurance opinion. The procedures we performed in carrying out our limited assurance in respect of Limited Assurance Sustainability Information, as per Appendix 1 (i), were based on our professional judgement and included: - Performing enquiries with respect to capturing, collating, calculating and reporting the Limited Assurance Sustainability Information; - Assessing the appropriateness of selected estimates, assumptions and methodologies applied by management in the preparation of the Limited Assurance Sustainability Information; - Calculating the arithmetic accuracy of a sample of calculations of the Limited Assurance Sustainability Information;

We have performed procedures as to whether these offsets were acquired during the year (or when actual emissions are unknown before the year end, until the issuance of the assurance report post year-end) and arrangements are in place for their surrender, as well as performed procedures over the calculation of net emissions. We have not, however, performed any procedures regarding the external providers of these offsets, and express no conclusion about whether the offsets have resulted, or will result, in a reduction of 1,000 tonnes of CO₂-e. The procedures we performed in carrying out our limited assurance in respect of the selected Limited Assurance Climate Information, as per Appendix 1 (iii), were based on our professional judgement and included: - Undertaking enquiries with management regarding the process and controls for capturing, collating and reporting the Limited Assurance Climate Information; - Agreeing a sample of lending exposures and their categorisation back to source systems and documentation; - Agreeing a sample of external data used in the estimation and attribution of emissions to third party sources (i.e. customers financial and non-financial data), however our scope did not include performing procedures over the underlying data provided by third-parties; - Assessing the reasonableness of any material estimates made in preparing the Limited Assurance Climate Information; - Reperforming a sample of calculations undertaken in preparing the selected Limited Assurance Climate Information and the appropriate application of the Climate Criteria in those calculations; and - Reviewing the presentations and disclosures of the selected Climate Subject Matter Information and Climate Criteria in the 2025 Annual Report. We believe that the evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our limited assurance conclusion.

## **Reasonable Assurance Sustainability Information** Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Reasonable Assurance Sustainability Information, as outlined in Appendix 1 (ii), based on the procedures we have performed and the evidence we have obtained. Our engagement has been conducted in accordance with the Australian Standard on Assurance Engagements (ASAE) 3000 _Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information_ and ASAE 3410 _Assurance Engagements on Greenhouse Gas Statements_ . Those standards require that we plan and perform this engagement to obtain reasonable assurance about whether anything has come to our attention to indicate that the Selected Sustainability Information has not been prepared, in all material respects, for the years ended or periods as at, as outlined in Appendix 1 (ii). A reasonable assurance engagement involves performing procedures to obtain evidence about the Reasonable Assurance Sustainability Information. The nature, timing and extent of procedures selected depend on professional judgement, including the assessment of risks of material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, in the Reasonable Assurance Sustainability Information. In making those risk assessments, we considered internal control relevant to the Group’s preparation of the Group’s Reasonable Assurance Sustainability Information. Our reasonable assurance engagement also included: - Evaluating the design and implementation of controls relevant to the selected Sustainability Information; and - Use of larger sample sizes for substantive procedures undertaken on a sample basis. We believe that the evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our reasonable assurance opinion.

## **Inherent limitations** **==> picture [71 x 35] intentionally omitted <==** of evolving knowledge and information to determine emissions factors and the values needed to combine emissions of different gases. It is acknowledged by stakeholders globally, including regulators, that there are significant limitations in the availability and quality of emissions data from third parties, resulting in the extensive use of proxy and third-party data. In addition, the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (“PCAF”) has established a ‘data quality score card’ and associate guidance for entities to measure their own data quality per asset class. The application of this data quality score card to determine a data quality score per asset class is inherently subjective. It is anticipated that the principles and methodologies used to measure and report the Climate Subject Matter Information will develop over time and may be subject to change in line with market practice and regulation, impacting comparability year-on-year. The uncertainties and limitations are laid out in more detail in the Climate Criteria. The assurance conclusion and opinion expressed in this report have been formed on the above basis.

## **Our limited assurance conclusion** Based on the procedures we have performed, as described under ‘Our responsibilities’ and the evidence we have obtained, nothing has come to our attention that causes us to believe that the Limited Assurance Sustainability Information and Limited Assurance Climate Information have not been prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the Sustainability and Climate criteria for the years ended or periods as at, as outlined in Appendices 1 (i) and (iii).

## **Emphasis of matter – Estimation of ‘Selected Scope 3 emissions’** The estimation of ‘Selected Scope 3 emissions’ within the Limited Assurance Sustainability Information, as per Appendix 1 (i), reported by the Group comprises selected sources of operational Scope 3 emissions only. We draw attention to the Climate disclosures appendix on pages 423 to 427 which sets out these assumptions and data sources for different Scope 3 emissions sources. Our conclusion is not modified in respect of this matter.

## **Risk management** The Board’s focus included the management of financial risks such as funding and liquidity, and non-financial risks, including fraud and scams, privacy and financial crime compliance. Key activities included: - Approving the risk management approach and changes to the risk appetite statement. - Overseeing the Bank’s Risk Management Framework, its operation by management, and receiving regular reports on financial and non-financial risk. - Approving revised risk-related policies including the Group Conflicts Management Policy, and the annual Group Aggregate Risk Exposures Policy and Group Liquidity Policy reviews. - Overseeing updates on implementation of CPS 230. - As required by APRA’s Prudential Standard CPS 220 _Risk Management_ (CPS 220), delivering an annual risk management declaration to APRA that the Risk Management Framework is adequately designed and operating effectively. - Monitoring the Bank’s risk culture. - Noting and discussing the key outcomes of the renewal of the Bank’s insurance program.

## **Fairer treatment of customers** The Board actively monitored a range of customer-related topics and initiatives this year. Key activities included: - Monitoring the progress of customer remediation initiatives. - Reviewing reporting on CBA’s performance on trust, reputation and brand, considering the link between trust and advocacy, and our broader contribution to the community. - Reviewing reports on customer complaints. - Monitoring the progress of the activities to reach our superior customer experience ambition. - Hearing from the Customer Advocate and the Chair of the Indigenous Advisory Council.

Key areas of focus included data, engineering productivity, financial crime, fraud and scams, relationship management and operations. Discussion also included the strategic alliance with Anthropic and the focus on aligning the AI strategy with our purpose of building a brighter future for all.**

## **Financial oversight** The Board remained focused on operational excellence and driving growth in its core banking businesses, as well as prudent balance sheet and capital management. Key activities included: - Monitoring the Bank’s operating performance. - Approving the FY24 full year and FY25 half year financial results. - Approving the FY24 final dividend and the FY25 interim dividend. - Receiving and considering regular reports from management in relation to the Bank’s funding, capital management and liquidity positions. - Noting and discussing simplification and cost strategies.

## **Environmental and social** The Board is responsible for considering the E&S impact of the Bank’s activities, overseeing adherence to the E&S Framework and approving climate-related disclosures. Key activities included: - Considering regular updates on the Bank’s E&S program. - Approving the 2024 Modern Slavery Statement. - Considering updates on the Bank’s social impact, including the Reconciliation Action Plan. - Considering and approving the FY26–28 Reconciliation Action Plan.

## **Capital management** **The Board is responsible for approving capital management initiatives. This year activities included approving the Bank’s internal capital adequacy assessment process, which assesses the Group’s current and future capital adequacy, and the Group’s plan and processes to manage its capital. The Board also approved changes to the Group Capital Policy and the Capital Management of Subsidiaries and Branches Policy.**

## **Hearing directly from our customers** **To better understand customer needs, the Board met with customers in Adelaide across sectors such as construction, building supplies, engineering, energy, retail and agriculture. These discussions offered valuable insights into our customers’ business operations, challenges, growth opportunities and what their expectations may be of CBA.**

## **Board performance, composition and renewal** The Board recognises the importance of having Directors with an appropriate mix of skills, experience and diversity to support sound decision making. As at 30 June 2025, the Board had 10 Directors: nine independent Non-Executive Directors and the CEO. With the assistance of the Nominations Committee, the Board regularly reviews its size and composition, and considers factors including independence, skills, experience and diversity of views.

## **Board renewal** Board renewal and orderly transitions are important for ensuring effective and sustainable Board performance. The Board skills matrix and the CBA Board Appointment, Renewal and Performance Policy frame the ongoing Board renewal process. These work together so that prescribed skills and experience are present within the Board and address the Bank’s existing and emerging strategic, business and governance issues. The Board remains focused on ongoing renewal and succession. Consideration is given to diversity, background, experience and skills. There have been several changes to the composition of the Board and certain Committees this year. Kate Howitt was appointed as an independent Non-Executive Director from 1 October 2024. Kate has significant experience in matters relating to strategy, capital allocation, stakeholder management and sustainability. Alistair Currie was appointed as an independent Non-Executive Director from 31 March 2025. Alistair has extensive international banking experience, having held roles in Australia, the United Kingdom, the United States, Asia and the Middle East. On 16 October 2024, Anne Templeman-Jones retired from the Board as an independent Non-Executive Director, Chair of the Audit Committee and member of the Risk & Compliance Committee. Following the retirement of Anne Templeman-Jones, Peter Harmer commenced as Chair of the Audit Committee, member of the Risk & Compliance Committee and stepped down from his role as a member of the People & Remuneration Committee. Lyn Cobley was subsequently appointed as a member of the People & Remuneration Committee.

## **Board performance evaluation** Continuously monitoring and improving its performance, as well as that of its Committees and individual Directors, remains important to the Board. Under its Charter, the Board must annually assess its performance and the performance of individual Directors. Additionally, an external performance review of the Board and Committees is required at least every three years. In 2024, an independent external evaluation assessed the performance of the Board, each Committee and individual Directors. The process included observation of Board meetings, and the completion of a survey and interviews with Directors, Executives, the Group Auditor and the Group Company Secretary. It also evaluated the effectiveness of Board and Committee processes, the appropriateness of meeting agendas, and the timeliness and adequacy of papers. The findings were presented to the Board in August 2024. An internal review was carried out in 2025. The process involved the completion of a survey by Directors, Executives, the Group Auditor and the Group Company Secretary covering matters such as roles and responsibilities, effectiveness, engagement and reporting. A performance review report was prepared and provided to the Board. The Chair also met with each of the participating Directors to share two-way feedback. **==> picture [71 x 10] intentionally omitted <==** **----- Start of picture text -----**

## **Board education and training** Providing Directors with opportunities to enhance their skills and knowledge is essential for them to perform effectively. The Nominations Committee is responsible for overseeing the Non-Executive Director induction program and appropriate continuing education opportunities for Directors, as well as periodically reviewing whether there is a need for existing Directors to undertake additional professional development.

## **Key components of Director training and education** **Induction program** Assists new Non-Executive Directors in understanding the Bank’s operations including governance, risk management, technology strategy and cyber security, E&S issues, audit, and regulatory and compliance matters. This year new Non-Executive Directors, Kate Howitt and Alistair Currie, attended customised induction programs, delivered as part of a multi-stage process. **Continuing** Incorporated into the Board calendar to enable Directors to develop and **education program** maintain skills and knowledge that support the Board’s decision making. To upskill our Board, targeted education sessions were provided which included presentations from external subject matter experts. Over the last 12 months this has covered topics such as Australia’s energy transition, technology modernisation and CPS 230. In addition, the Board participated in an educational trip to Asia to explore topics relevant to CBA’s context. This is an important part of the Board’s annual strategy calendar, serving as a source of new ideas and learning. **Annual directors’** Provided to all Directors. **duties training** This year included a refresher on key directors’ duties and evolving areas such as cyber, AI and CPS 230. Additional training was also provided on the Financial Accountability Regime, whistleblowing and key regulatory obligations. **Group mandatory** Directors are required to complete training on Group policies. In 2025 this **learning** included topics such as financial crime compliance, privacy, workplace health and safety, information security including cyber security, our Code of Conduct and conflicts of interest.

## **Managing our risks** Effective risk management enables us to fulfil our purpose of building a brighter future for all. Our embedded risk framework, together with a strong culture, empowers our people to take the right risks to deliver better outcomes for our customers and communities.
## **Risk management in action** The Board-approved risk appetite statement (RAS) establishes the level of risk we must operate in to deliver our strategy.

## **Our Risk Management Framework enablers** Our Risk Management Framework (RMF) outlines the Bank’s expectations on how we identify, measure, monitor and respond to our risks. The RMF enablers facilitate the effective identification, measurement, monitoring and response to our material risks. Our RMF is comprised of systems, structures, policies, processes and people. They work together to help identify, assess and mitigate our internal and external sources of risk. **Risk policies and procedures** We categorise the material risks the Bank is exposed to as strategic, financial and non-financial risks. Each material risk type has its own specific framework or requirements to manage the risk. **Risk accountabilities and skills** **Risk governance and reporting Risk infrastructure and data** These material risks and our approach to managing them are set out in our RMF. The RMF is reviewed annually by the ELT and the Board. The RMF is also independently reviewed every three years by an external reviewer, supported by internal and external audit programs. These reviews of the RMF as well as our annual RMD to APRA, set out our plans to strengthen the RMF in support of our strategy.

## **Risk policies and procedures** Our risk policies and procedures outline the principles and practices to help us to identify and assess our material risks. They help us translate the RAS into our daily business activities.

## **Risk governance and reporting** The Board has ultimate responsibility for the Bank’s risk governance, including the RMF and its implementation by management. The Board is supported by its four Committees as well as management-level committees that oversee our material risks. Management regularly provides information to the Board which allows material risk positions to be monitored against the RAS and policy limits.

## **Risk accountabilities and skills** The Three Lines of Accountability model (3LoA) organises our accountabilities to manage the Bank’s risks by separating the roles. Line 1 own and manage the risks whereas Line 2 develop risk frameworks and provide assurance. Line 3 provide independent assurance over how effectively risks are being managed. The 3LoA include skilled employees within each line and are supported by risk capabilities, and performance and remuneration frameworks. Our remuneration framework supports accountability by incorporating risk assessment as gate openers and modifiers in employee and executive remuneration.
## **Risk infrastructure and data** Our risk infrastructure provides the systems, tools, models and data required for the effective management of our material risks.

## **Risk appetite** The RAS is reviewed and approved annually by the Board in line with our operating context, and is adapted for new and changing risks present in our operations. The Board-approved RAS helps embed a culture focused on disciplined risk management to enable smart risk taking. The RAS also includes key risk indicators for our material risks. This provides signals for building levels of risk and encourages management to take action and avoid a breach of appetite. In addition to governance of RAS performance through Board and management-level committees, our Group policies, procedures, delegations and limits translate and embed the RAS into our daily business activities.

## **Risk culture** Our risk culture reflects our beliefs and behaviours within the Bank and determines how we identify, measure, monitor and respond to risks. These behaviours guide decision making and good risk management, and embody our values and leadership principles. This helps our actions align to our core beliefs. To sustain and improve our risk culture, senior management and the Board form a view of the Bank’s risk culture through an annual Board risk culture assessment. This is supported by the Group risk culture response plan, which addresses areas of focus identified by the Board. It is further reinforced by self-reflections on business unit risk culture to drive improvement at the team level.

## **Risk measurement** We use multiple techniques to identify and measure risks the Bank is exposed to. These include stress testing and scenario analysis; risk and control self-assessments; compliance self-assessments; emerging risk assessment; systems and models to quantify risks and identify risk exceptions; assurance of the RMF in the form of Line 1 controls testing; Line 2 assurance reviews and framework approvals; Line 3 internal audits; and the external audit program.

## **Stress testing** Stress testing and scenario analysis are important risk management tools. They enable the Board and senior management to better understand, quantify and manage risks. They also inform how we may respond to risk events occurring and any potential weaknesses in our actions during a crisis. The results of these stress tests are important for strengthening our risk management approach. Stress testing results also inform our risk appetite and assist us in identifying the acceptable levels of risk we will assume in our operations.

## **Manage and control risks** We implement measures to manage and control risks within appetite such as: detective and preventative controls; limits; delegated authorities and review and approval processes; policies and procedures; and issue and incident management. The 3LoA model organises our risk accountabilities by separating the roles for managing the Bank’s risks. **For more information on the Bank’s RMF and risk types, see Note 9 on pages 303–344 in the** _**Financial report**_ **.**

## **Risk management oversight** The Board has ultimate responsibility for the Bank’s risk governance, including the RMF and oversight of its operation by management. The Board is supported by the Risk & Compliance Committee, Audit Committee, Nominations Committee and People & Remuneration Committee, as well as specific management-level committees that oversee material risks. Each year the Board assesses the maturity of our RMF in managing our material risks through our RMD, and adjusts the RMF as required. Together with the setting of risk appetite, this helps the Bank maintain a risk management framework that is fit for our business size, operating context and delivery of our strategic priorities. Our RMD to APRA allows the Board to reflect on the framework’s design and operating effectiveness and adjust, where needed. Committees assist the Board to fulfil its roles and responsibilities. Committees meet to consider and discuss specific matters in detail and, where appropriate, make recommendations to the Board for resolution. Processes are in place to support effective and timely information flows between Committees and provide the Board with clear oversight of matters. **For more information on our corporate governance structure and committees, see page 38.**

## **Board Risk & Compliance Committee** **The Board Risk & Compliance Committee reviews and oversees the RMF and adherence to the Bank’s Board-approved risk appetite. The Committee monitors our risk profile against changes in our operating context. Management provides regular reports to the Committee to provide oversight of current and emerging risks, the effectiveness of our control environment and our risk management practices.** **and scams, operational resilience, privacy, data, environmental and social, artificial intelligence and financial crime compliance.** **The Risk & Compliance Committee meets six times per year, or more frequently if needed, with the Chair of the Committee reporting to the Board after each Committee meeting. The Committee also supports the Board’s concurrent meetings. It provides updates on relevant risk outcomes and matters at the concurrent meetings to support the assessment of remuneration outcomes for the CEO and Group Executives and performance outcomes of the Group Auditor.** **It is important for directors to spend the right amount of time on the right issues. This year the Committee’s focus remained on the management of financial risks such as funding and liquidity, and non-financial and strategic risks, including cyber security, fraud**

## **Risk Management Declaration** **Each year the Board makes a RMD to APRA to meet the requirements of APRA’s CPS 220, confirming the RMF remains fit for managing our material risks, or outlines steps to strengthen the RMF. Lines 1 and 2, with an opinion from Line 3 and collective agreement by the ELT, form a recommendation on the RMD to the Board Risk & Compliance Committee. This supports the Directors to determine whether the RMF is adequately designed and operating effectively in all material respects. This year particular attention was given to protecting our customers through strengthening our RMF to help reduce fraud, scams, cyber threats, financial crime, and business disruption and to support the Bank’s responsible use of AI. This focus reflects the evolving threat landscape and reinforces our commitment to strengthening the resilience of our organisation to deliver our strategy.**

## **Our risk management committees** At management level, risk governance is undertaken by a structured hierarchy of individual accountabilities, personal delegations, management committees and forums across the Bank. Management regularly monitors financial, strategic and non-financial risk exposures against the Bank’s RAS and policy limits. This information is provided to the Board Committees in the form of Board papers, which are prepared and shared with the Board Committees on a bi-monthly basis. Following management committee meetings, papers are shared with Board Committees for noting, approval or discussion. This flow of information is essential for management committees to effectively support the Board.

## **Executive Leadership Team** The ELT is accountable for developing and executing the Bank’s strategy and supports the Board by advising on strategic risks and opportunities, including those related to technology. This year the ELT increased its focus on accelerating the modernisation of the Bank’s technology estate to strengthen technology stability, security and operational continuity. Modernisation also supports the use of new tools, technologies and AI, and delivery of enhanced customer experiences. The ELT has set the strategic direction, allocated the required capacity and capability, and maintained oversight of progress against execution priorities. **Chaired by: Chief Executive Officer** **Meets: Weekly or as required** The ELT is responsible for making specific recommendations to the CEO and agreeing common actions addressing strategy, business performance, people leadership and culture, and risk and compliance management and control. The ELT may establish committees to assist it in carrying out its functions.

## **Financial Risk Committee** The FRC supports the Board by overseeing the Bank’s financial risk frameworks with oversight of the governance, key credit risk principles and policies that apply to the Group. On a continuing basis during the year, various discussion papers are submitted to the FRC for review in response to emerging financial risks and changes to the credit environment, including but not limited to, global geopolitical developments that may impact the Bank and its customers. The committee assesses whether to make adjustments to our risk appetite and/or the Group Credit Risk Framework. **Chaired by: Chief Risk Officer** **Meets: Monthly** The Financial Risk Committee (FRC) assists and advises the CEO on the governance, optimisation and effective management of the Bank’s financial risks in accordance with the RAS and RMF.

## **Asset and Liability Committee** **Chaired by: Chief Financial Officer Meets: Monthly** The Asset and Liability Committee (ALCO) oversees the Group’s balance sheet settings and the effective management of the Bank’s non-traded market risk, interest rate risk, liquidity, funding, capital and structural foreign exchange risk.

## **Non-Financial Risk Committee** The NFRC discussed requirements of CPS 230, including Board and management accountabilities, and plans to achieve compliance. Leading up to the effective date of 1 July 2025, the Committee reviewed the Business Continuity Plan summaries, including associated tolerances of the Bank’s critical operations ahead of review by the Board Risk & Compliance Committee. **Chaired by: Chief Executive Officer Meets: Bi-monthly** The Non-Financial Risk Committee (NFRC) advises the CEO on the governance, optimisation and effective management of the Bank’s non-financial risks in accordance with the RAS and RMF.

## **Risk & Remuneration Review Committee** **Chaired by: Chief Risk Officer Meets: Quarterly** The Group Risk & Remuneration Review Committee advises the Group Chief Risk Officer on risk considerations for determining remuneration outcomes in line with the Group Remuneration Policy. This assists the Group Chief Risk Officer to support the Chief Executive Officer and Board to determine remuneration outcomes across the Bank.

## **Our emerging risks** While remaining vigilant to the risks we need to manage today, we also look ahead to identify potential future challenges. We aim to uphold the risk management standards expected by our customers, communities, regulators and shareholders, both now and in the future. Emerging risks are risks that are either newly developing or already exist, but their effects have not yet been substantially realised. These risks are often constantly evolving and have the potential to impact the Bank and our customers in the medium to long term (over 12 months). It is essential to respond to these risks now to minimise their potential future impact. Emerging risks are often driven by new trends in our operating environment, such as competition, new technologies, regulation or evolving customer expectations. Our emerging risk profile is updated annually through a review process with the ELT and the Board. This process aligns with the annual review of the Bank’s strategy. The emerging risk process evaluates the adequacy of the Bank’s mitigation strategies to prevent emerging risks from materially impacting the Bank. In cases where we may have limited ability to influence emerging risks, it may be more challenging to implement effective mitigative actions. This may require us to take additional steps to address these risks. The emerging risk themes the Board and ELT focused on this year are outlined below.

## **macroeconomic uncertainty** Upcoming regulatory reforms could significantly impact us and our customers, spanning areas like Anti-Money Laundering/Counter-Terrorism Financing (AML/CTF), cyber security, scams, privacy, payments licensing, AI and climate disclosures. To prepare for new regulation, we frequently evaluate our obligations including those under the new _Scam Prevention Framework Act 2025 (Cth)_ , which will be further supported by industry specific codes, not yet released. The Bank is also improving its security infrastructure for fraud and scams, and forming partnerships to better handle scam phishing and reporting within the industry ecosystem. Our operations face risks from global political events, such as elections and policy changes, civil unrest, international competition and conflicts. These disruptions can increase social pressures domestically; affect unemployment, housing supply, and market volatility; and escalate credit and operational risks for financial institutions. Failure to prepare for these geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainties could heighten our exposure to various financial and non-financial risks, which we monitor and manage through our RMF.

## **Emerging technology** Australia’s economy needs affordable and reliable energy. Replacing coal-fired power with firmed renewable energy is crucial to meet Australia’s renewable energy targets. With 90% of coal-fired power stations expected to retire by 2035, delays in replacement generation could increase electricity price volatility, affect reliability and have broader economic impacts. Credit risks could also be heightened for the Bank, as well as disruptions to our operations. We continue to engage with Government on the energy transition and support retail and business customers finance existing technologies, such as rooftop solar, batteries and electric vehicles to help reduce their emissions. This also helps reduce reliance on large-scale utility investments. Innovation driven by emerging and disruptive technology, including AI, continues to rapidly evolve. As we pursue our strategy, which includes a focus on technology and AI, we continue working hard to effectively manage risks from change implementation that could lead to service disruptions, poor customer experiences, fraud and scams, conduct issues, cyber security threats, and data and privacy issues. As a Bank, we invest in governance and risk initiatives to support our AI goals, including for responsible AI.

## **Cyber security threats** The Bank anticipates cyber attacks to persist and grow as adversaries use new technologies such as GenAI to exploit vulnerabilities, including third parties and cloud environments. These could lead to compromised customer data, critical systems disruptions and potential breaches of our obligations. We continue to strengthen our cyber security risk management through dedicated teams that monitor and respond to potential cyber security threats, applying learnings from the Board and senior management crisis management exercises, and a focus on enhancing our cyber security control environment to address emerging threats.

## **Growing societal pressures impacting our customers and communities** The Bank continues to face heightened expectations from governments, regulators and the community to respond to key challenges including cost-of-living pressures, housing affordability and crisis support. Many Australians are feeling the impact of rising fraud and scams activity, as well as ongoing affordability concerns. We remain focused on supporting our customers through these challenges and continue to invest in strengthening our fraud and scams infrastructure to help keep them safe.

## **Understanding stakeholder views on climate change** We recognise the importance of balancing diverse stakeholder views to evaluate risks and opportunities, and drive more informed decision making and disclosures, particularly on sustainability issues. We proactively engage with our key stakeholders to understand their perspectives, build trusted relationships, and gather insights that can help shape our products and services. Stakeholder insights also inform our materiality assessment, which identifies the sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities most important to our stakeholders and the Bank. We acknowledge that climate change is a collective challenge and we actively engage with our stakeholders to understand their diverse perspectives. Our key stakeholders are individuals and groups in our value chain whose interests are, or could be, materially impacted by the Bank’s activities. Guided by our values and Code of Conduct, we engage with key stakeholders through our regular business activities and dedicated feedback channels. Stakeholder insights are shared through internal forums and committees to support informed decision making across the Bank.

## **This includes:** **• Engaging with customers and providing products and services to help them transition and build climate resilience.** **• Engaging with investors to understand their climate-related priorities. This helps to inform our strategy, reporting and deliver long-term sustainable returns for our shareholders.** Engagement with customers, communities, government and regulators helps us to consider opportunities to support financial inclusion and enhance customer outcomes. For example, stakeholder channels such as the CBA Community Council, Indigenous Advisory Council and Modern Slavery Advisory Council connect us to community groups and can help inform our response to issues such as financial abuse, artificial intelligence (AI) and customer vulnerability. - **Working with and assessing our supply chain to monitor and reduce supply chain-related emissions.** We continue to enhance our stakeholder engagement by improving how insights are shared across the Bank. Stakeholder insights help to inform our operational and strategic priorities, as well as the development of products and services.

## **• Partnering with external** **organisations, participating in industry associations and advocating for public policies that support affordable and reliable clean energy and economic resilience.** > **[See our stakeholder engagement approach at commbank.com.au][/p][olicies]** > **[For more information on how we are supporting our customers, see ][pages 74][–][77][.]** > **[For more information about how the Board engages with stakeholders, see ][page][ 4][6][. ]** **==> picture [287 x 230] intentionally omitted <==** - **Collaborating with research partners to develop and share insights on climate change.** - **Meeting with external groups and agencies to hear their views on the energy transition and our role as a lender.** **==> picture [9 x 387] intentionally omitted <==**

We engage with our people to understand how they feel about work and their wellbeing. This also helps us understand their level of engagement. We conduct surveys and engage through employee forums, town halls and employee-led networks.

## **Improving our materiality assessment** Our annual materiality assessment seeks to identify sustainability topics that are most relevant to our stakeholders and CBA. Insights from the assessment are shared across the Bank and with the Board, to help inform decision making and our sustainability disclosures. **Our materiality assessment process Identify initial longlist of topics Review operating context, industry trends, peer insights, macrotrends, sustainability trends and regulatory environment. 1 Filter list for relevance Conduct internal analysis and interviews with internal subject matter experts. Align with sustainability and materiality assessment frameworks to capture material topics. 2 Filter list for importance Internal subject matter experts rate topics by (1) ability to impact the economy, environment and people; (2) CBA’s ability to influence the topic; and (3) financial materiality. Use the Bank’s 5x5 risk matrix to guide ratings. 3 Filter list for materiality Senior management review and validate prioritised topics considering both impact and financial materiality. Group topics into material themes. 4 Report on material themes Share insights across the Bank and with the Board. Use material themes to guide annual reporting, disclosing material sustainability-related themes which matter most to our key stakeholders and CBA. 5** The assessment considers CBA’s operating environment and uses insights from our stakeholder engagement. Internal subject matter experts, representing key stakeholder groups, assess proposed topics based on their direct engagement with stakeholders. Each topic is evaluated for its relevance to Australia’s economy, environment and people, and CBA’s impact on or ability to influence the topic (impact materiality), as well as the topic’s potential impact on CBA’s financial performance (financial materiality). Guided by global frameworks such as the Global Reporting Initiative and Sustainability Accounting Standards Board, our materiality assessment requires significant judgement and is a qualitative assessment. It considers a range of sustainability topics through research, stakeholder interviews and workshops with senior management. This year we enhanced our materiality assessment process to better identify topics that are potentially financially material for CBA. We also aligned our impact assessment scale to the Bank’s 5x5 risk matrix, enabling us to assess and prioritise material topics more consistently. Our assessment will continue to evolve in line with emerging guidance to improve how we identify material sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities.

## **Understanding this year’s material themes** The new Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards present an opportunity for us to enhance how we address material sustainability issues, while improving the transparency, consistency and comparability of our sustainability disclosures over time. Our material themes and underlying topics remain aligned with the strategic priorities, material risks and themes outlined in our 2024 Annual Report. Customer experience, support and community impact continue to be top priorities for both stakeholders and CBA. This year underlying topics such as fraud and scams, cost of living, payments, customer experience and housing affordability gained importance. Access to banking also rose in importance, driven by an increased focus on cash and branch availability in regional Australia. Our report is structured around material themes that reflect our most significant sustainability topics for the year. The theme ‘Banking strategy, operations and operating context’ is not presented as a standalone material theme. While core to the Bank’s strategy and financial performance, we have not classified it as a sustainability topic and it is not expected to be assessed as a separate sustainability theme in future years. Given the theme is inherently material to the Bank, our approach and activities are disclosed in other sections of this report. Stakeholders reaffirmed that a supported and engaged workforce is essential to CBA’s value creation. CBA plays a key role in shaping employee engagement and wellbeing, and fostering a workplace culture that is safe, respectful and inclusive. As digitisation and AI reshape the workforce, the need for reskilling and upskilling is growing, though stakeholders also noted people skills remain vital for customer-facing roles. > **[For more information on material topics related to our material ] themes, see pages 74–93.** > **[For more information on how our material themes are mapped ] to material risks, see pages 65–67.**

text: ## **Learning from customer feedback** Customer insights from a range of sources help us understand what is working well and where there are opportunities to improve. **In response to customer dissatisfaction around fraudulent transactions, we have increased fraud alerts to 35,000 per day and integrated them with a self-service tool. We now identify the majority of fraudulent transactions and enable customers to lodge disputes in a matter of minutes without the need to call or message us or go to a branch.** We use customer experience surveys to capture feedback, monitor trends and understand how customers engage with us. We also monitor operational metrics, including complaints, disputes, wait times and service availability, providing useful indicators of areas requiring attention. These metrics together with the Net Promoter Score (NPS), an external measure of customer advocacy, give us a benchmark to improve on. We are prioritising key experiences across consumer and small business banking and are embedding a new approach to collecting direct customer feedback. This approach seeks to provide a more complete and consistent understanding of customer experiences, helping us better focus on outcomes for our customers. **Feedback from customers, particularly those unable to visit a branch, also led us to digitise the lodgement process for Power Of Attorneys and Financial Management Orders. This inclusive shift has improved efficiency and convenience, with over 90% of lodgements now made online.** We are also exploring ways to gain deeper customer insights. We have now entered our second year of a program that to-date has observed financial behaviours and decisions inside the homes of over 70 young adult Australians across 10 locations. Early insights indicate young adults often rely on non-bank tools to manage finances, revealing unmet needs with their primary bank.

## **Measuring customer experience** We currently hold the #1 NPS ranking across major banks in the Consumer, Business and Digital categories, and have held this ranking across all for at least 11 months. This year our Institutional NPS ranking has dropped to #2 after previously holding the #1 ranking for 24 consecutive months. There is still more work to do to improve our NPS scores. Detailed reports on the drivers of NPS can be accessed by our people to understand what is influencing the absolute scores. This change highlights the importance of focusing on continuously improving our service and prioritising the customer in everything we do.
