## **Supporting customers in severe weather events** **Using customer feedback and internal data, we developed the Disaster Resilience Toolkit. The toolkit introduces a suite of tools and resources to help support our customers before, during and after a weather-related event. We also take steps to avoid adding unnecessary stress. For example, our Business Banking team temporarily removed automated late payment reminders for around 14,000 customers in communities affected by natural disasters this year. We also donated $100,000 to Rural Aid to fund the delivery of critical resources and services to more rural Australian communities impacted by severe weather events.** > **[See more about emergency and disaster assistance at commbank.com.au/naturaldisasters]** 76 OUR APPROACH TO SUSTAINABILITY 77

## **Making banking safer for our customers** **==> picture [122 x 245] intentionally omitted <==** Fraud, scams, cyber threats and financial crime continue to impact many Australians. We have more work to do and remain focused on investing to help protect our customers and communities. More customers than ever are choosing to engage with us through the CommBank app. We are balancing transaction speed with the need for a streamlined, safe and secure digital payment experience. New warnings for first-time payments through NetBank and the CommBank app now provide enhanced alerts for customers. Increased alerting helped to reduce customer-reported fraud by 40% over the year. We also introduced a feature in the CommBank app that allows customers to see all digital wallets their payment details have been linked to and remove any they do not recognise. More than 1.3 million customers have used this feature since launch in August 2024. We have seen a 30% reduction in customer scam losses year-on-year supported by initiatives including behavioural security, NameCheck, CallerCheck and CustomerCheck. To further strengthen account protection, we introduced a new multi-factor authentication process for NetBank, requiring customers to confirm login attempts via the app. This added security layer helps prevent unauthorised access, even in cases where a user’s password has been comprised. > **[For more information on cyber, privacy and data management, see ][p][a][g][es 89–91.]**

## **How can I help?** We actively engage with customers to provide information about evolving fraud and scams threats. This year the Bank reached out to customers through NetBank, the CommBank app, news articles, social media, in-branch community sessions and campaigns. > **[Have regular conversations about ] scams with family and friends.** > **[Stay informed about the latest ] scam tactics.** Research commissioned by CBA revealed that while 90% of Australians believe that talking about scams with loved ones can raise awareness, only 8% felt comfortable having a discussion with family about being scammed. To help bridge this gap, CBA launched a new education campaign that aims to encourage conversations about the dangers of scams between generations. By addressing intergenerational knowledge gaps, it seeks to empower all Australians, particularly older generations, with the information and tools needed to help them stay safe. > **[Remember to implement and ] educate others on three simple steps to help prevent scams:** **1. Stop: Does a call, email or text seem off? The best thing to do is stop and take a breath. Real organisations will not put you under pressure to act instantly.** **==> picture [278 x 188] intentionally omitted <==** **2. Check: Ask someone you trust or contact the organisation the message claims to be from.** **3. Reject: If unsure, hang up on the caller, delete the email, block the phone number. Change your password if you think someone else may have it, and make sure you pick something long and unique.** **Contact your bank immediately if you suspect a scam.** **See more about the campaign and how to stay safe from scams at commbank.com.au/ scam-tips**

## **Supporting financial inclusion** As Australia’s largest bank, it is important that we provide tailored and accessible solutions to promote the financial inclusion of our customers and communities.

## **Improving access to banking** We aim to provide products and services that meet the diverse needs of our customers and provide equitable access to help them achieve their financial goals. We recognise there are systemic barriers to banking and financial inclusion experienced by some members of the community, and we are committed to understanding and removing these barriers so more Australians can access banking confidently, independently and with dignity. We are fortunate to have one in two new migrants to Australia trust us with their banking needs and recognise the unique challenges they face. This year we updated and improved our Moving to Australia online resources, which provide practical guidance on opening bank accounts, managing money and accessing digital tools – designed to support a confident start to life in Australia. To better support our customers who hold eligible government concession cards, we offer a basic bank account, our Streamline Basic account, which has no monthly account keeping, overdraw or dishonour fees. Improving financial inclusion for First Nations customers and communities remains a priority. Alongside our branch teams and Indigenous Customer Assistance Line, Indigenous Business Banking team, and Indigenous banking concierge offer support tailored to community needs. We are also focused on building strong financial awareness and habits in children. Kit, our pocket money app for kids, used by over 100,000 customers, helps improve financial capability through fun and interactive learning. This year we introduced linking between interest-earning CommBank Youthsaver accounts and Kit, allowing kids to transfer and see their money grow. We also offer Minor Trust accounts through CommSec, allowing parents to hold investments on behalf of their children to help build their financial future.

## **Continuing to support our regional communities** **==> picture [166 x 249] intentionally omitted <==** We continue to support regional Australia with over 40% of our branch network located in regional areas. We maintained the biggest branch network in regional Australia and extended the CBA-branded regional branch closure moratorium until the end of July 2027. Our Bank@Post partnership with Australia Post also helps our customers, especially those in rural and regional areas, to continue having access to face-to-face banking services. There are more than 3,300 Bank@Post outlets across Australia, including in over 1,100 communities where there is no bank branch of any kind. To deepen our relationship with regional customers and communities we continued our regional growth initiative. This initiative connects business bankers with our branch network to support regional advocacy, customer engagement and brand awareness. CBA also sponsored the National Bush Summit, a national campaign advocating for regional and rural Australia, addressing important issues like cost of living, fraud and scams, and the future of farming and agriculture. We also aim to help more regional Australians stay safe online. We offered regional Australians access to more than 600 ‘Staying Safe Online’ education sessions this year. By partnering with local community groups to expand accessibility to the program, we delivered more than 300 of these free sessions in community centres in regional towns allowing more people to attend, no matter who they bank with.

## **Recognising and supporting customers with hidden disabilities** As part of the Bank’s ongoing commitment to deliver more inclusive products and experiences, we joined the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower program. A discreet symbol, worn as a pin, lanyard or wristband, allows people to voluntarily share with others that they have a disability or condition that may not be immediately apparent, and that they may need extra support. We provide training to our retail frontline teams to help them recognise and support customers with a hidden disability or non-visible condition, and we encourage our customers to wear the symbol if they feel comfortable to do so. The Hidden Disabilities Sunflower program complements our Equal Access Toolkit, used in all CBA branches and includes practical tools to support customers who may need an adjusted experience to complete a task in branch independently. We have also recently launched a new webpage for our neurodivergent customers. **See more about neuroinclusive banking at commbank.com.au/neuroinclusivebanking**

## **Helping address financial abuse** has supported 12,589 participants to help them feel more confident with money, regain control over their finances and plan for the future. We have reaffirmed our partnership with Good Shepherd Australia New Zealand from July 2024 until June 2028 to continue supporting FIH participants on their road to long-term financial independence. Our Next Chapter program is our long-term commitment to help address domestic and family violence (DFV) and financial abuse in Australia. Our Next Chapter team continues to provide free and confidential support to victim survivors of DFV and financial abuse, no matter who they bank with. This year the Next Chapter team provided support through over 18,500 individual interactions. We also continued to block transactions due to abusive language, stopping over 320,000 transactions this year. Our AI model continues to identify over 3,600 cases each year which are further reviewed by our Next Chapter team. We support selected not-for-profit organisations delivering innovative responses to financial abuse recovery through our Next Chapter Innovation program. This year we launched the second cohort of the Next Chapter Innovation program, specifically focused on helping to address financial abuse in First Nations communities. We have provided more than $1 million to date through Next Chapter Innovation together with a range of non-financial support, including executive support and mentoring, to help accelerate innovative responses to financial abuse. The Financial Independence Hub (FIH) delivered by Good Shepherd Australia New Zealand and funded by CBA, continues to provide free, confidential and ongoing support for people who have experienced financial abuse, regardless of who they bank with. ## **Enabling First Nations economic aspirations** The Bank has a longstanding commitment to reconciliation, having launched our first Reconciliation Action Plan (RAP) in 2008. text: ## **Recognising our people** **Our annual excellence awards recognise our people who reflect our values and leadership principles, and the behaviours, including risk management, that will help us achieve our customer ambition. The excellence awards align with our cultural priorities, recognising breakthrough outcomes, impactful learning and customer excellence.** **One of this year’s award winners, Gijo Mathew, was recognised for his role in rebuilding an automated verification system for home loans and accelerating the digital home loan approval process, creating a much better experience for our customers and people.**

## **Attracting talent and developing key pipelines** To help us deliver our strategy we continue to prioritise talent attraction and retention, particularly for critical skills in technology. We are committed to creating a culture of continuous learning so that our people can continue to grow and develop, and we remain a workplace of choice for key talent. To attract and retain the right people, we are differentiating our experience by providing personalised progression with pathways to upskill, reskill and grow careers. We are focused on developing talent pipelines, including through our graduate program and our career comeback program. This year we welcomed 350 graduates into the program with over 200 in technology and have expanded our career comeback program into engineering and financial crime. Since 2021, 43 individuals have been placed in our career comeback program with 97% offered employment upon completion. Building awareness and early engagement with students remains a focus, sponsoring community initiatives targeting potential talent through Girls in Tech, She Codes, Day of AI, ABCN Tech Programs, Vogue Codes and CSIRO Young Indigenous Women in STEM programs. Recognising the importance of diverse talent pipelines, we continue to explore alternative pathways to secure entry-level technology talent. We have adopted the T-EDI Standards, a data-driven set of principles to support inclusion in technology. We have also made a commitment with the NSW Digital Skills and Workforce Compact to hire 20% of entry-level technology talent through alternate pathways by 2030.

## **Investing in future skills** Technology and customer expectations continue to reshape our ways of working. We want our people to learn, build and apply the skills that prepare us for the future of work. We continue to empower our people with scaled access to the latest AI products, including more than 17,500 of our people granted access to Copilot. With more of our people now accessing AI tools in their role, it is important that we help them to use the technology responsibly and effectively to drive better customer outcomes. Our approach to upskilling and reskilling remains focused on the technical, behavioural and leadership skills required to deliver our strategy and manage risk.

## **Reskilling in Business Banking** Our ‘AI for All’ and ‘AI Deep Dive’ micro learning series continues to help our people learn what AI is and how to use it responsibly. There have been over 100,000 module engagements on AI this year, with 98% of survey respondents saying they have a better understanding of AI. However, human skills such as leadership, empathy, good judgement and smart risk taking remain key focus areas in our skilling strategy.

## **160+** **reskilled with 62% securing next role** We continue to invest in community skilling that helps build strong, diverse talent pipelines for the Bank and Australia. We continued our partnership with Year 13, which offers free and easily accessible programs for young Australians. This year we launched a career tools program on human skills that are resilient to technological advancements and will become even more important for employability. With the pace of technological change and AI advancement, the program aims to help high school students identify the skills they have, learn how to articulate those key skills and build on them.
## **1.1m** **students, parents and advisors reached through the human skills program activity** **==> picture [207 x 127] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Upskilling and reskilling our people** **To help our people build future skills we have delivered a range of upskilling and reskilling initiatives in partnership with UNSW. We have reskilled over 160 people for frontline Business Banking roles with 62% securing their next opportunity internally. More than 640 of our people participated in our Advance Analytics upskilling program, receiving a digital certificate.**

## **Reflecting the customers and communities we serve** We recognise the value in diversity of thought and having a team that reflects the customers and communities we serve. We want to create an environment where everyone feels included, safe and respected at work. As we work towards this, we are focused on initiatives which strengthen inclusion and prevent behaviours and norms that can normalise disrespect and lead to inequality. Our business unit inclusion and diversity councils and seven employee diversity networks support the execution of our strategy by providing feedback and lived experience. This year we reviewed our 2025-2028 Diversity, Equity and Inclusion strategy. We reset and aligned our diversity goals across gender equality, Indigenous workforce representation and cultural diversity. While we have made progress, there is more to do. We have set 2028 as the target date for these refreshed goals. We are working towards achieving 47-50% gender equality in Executive Manager and above roles, having reached 45.1% this year. Our goal of 3% Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander representation in our domestic workforce remains a focus, with current representation at 1.4%. We are also aiming for 40% cultural diversity in Executive Manager and above roles, with representation at 39.0% this year. The Bank remains committed to improving gender equality outcomes. We continue to see a lower proportion of women in senior and higher-paying technical specialist roles, which is reflected in our Workplace Gender Equality Agency (WGEA) median gender pay gap of 26.8% and average gender pay gap of 21.3% as at 31 March 2025. We will continue to work to reduce our gender pay gap across the Bank and continue taking action to accelerate progress. > **[See more about how we are reducing our gender pay gap in our CBA Em][p][lo][y][er Statement.]** > **[See more about our commitment to inclusion and diversity at ][co][mm][ba][nk.][co][m.][au/d][iv][e][r][s][i][ty]**

text: ## **Fostering employee wellbeing** We are committed to providing a positive and supportive environment where our people feel safe and respected at work. Our protect, care and thrive model helps guide our decision making.

## **Thrive** We care for our people’s health and wellbeing and want them to feel comfortable bringing their whole selves to work. We want to protect our people, customers and communities by reviewing and improving our programs to mitigate risk and minimise harm. We want to optimise our people’s potential, performance and prosperity. To learn and get better every day, we actively engage with our teams to understand how to improve the wellbeing experience and deliver the right tools, learning resources and assistance to help our people reach their full potential. Our people-centred approach is informed by data, driving early detection of potential issues, risk profiling that delivers predictive and preventative insights, and evidence-based solutions. We conduct regular health, safety and wellbeing assessments across our domestic and international offices, including targeted reviews in high-risk environments to improve safety maturity. Leadership is key to supporting our people in feeling physically and psychologically safe at work. Leadership capability is a key focus and leaders are encouraged to engage in wellbeing conversations, including how to refer team members to appropriate support. The Financial Fitness program aims to equip our people with the knowledge and practical steps needed to take control of their finances and pave the way for a brighter financial future. Through a series of engaging and interactive exercises, the program helps strengthen savings habits and supports our people in setting and achieving meaningful financial goals. A dedicated early intervention team supports our people with physical and mental health, and wellbeing-related issues. We have enhanced the support provided to our people experiencing difficult situations such as DFV or financial distress. This year we have also launched a GP and telehealth service, providing all our people with easy, direct access to healthcare services at no cost. All employees are required to complete mandatory training which reinforces their responsibilities in maintaining a safe, respectful and inclusive workplace. The training covers hazard identification, duty of care and how to escalate concerns appropriately.

## **Governance, culture and accountability** We aim to manage our business responsibly with a culture that requires us to do what is right to meet our customer and community expectations, and regulatory obligations.

## **Supporting better customer and community outcomes** One in three Australians and one in four businesses trust us as their main financial institution. Caring for our customers, communities and one another, having the courage to lead by example, and demonstrating our commitment to doing what is right is how we earn trust. We introduced our Code of Conduct in 2018 to guide our decision making in every situation and embed our values across the whole organisation. Since then, it has become an essential part of helping us do what is right and to help deliver fairer and ethical outcomes for our customers, especially when we face difficult decisions. As we are committed to learning and getting better every day, we updated our Code of Conduct this year. The changes reflect what we have learned from recent experiences where we did not get the right outcome for our customers. Where expectations have changed and customers have been impacted, we may go back and undertake reviews; where we did not get the right outcome for our customers, we will remediate to make things right. The code is designed to help strengthen both how we meet our legal and regulatory obligations, and how we act ethically and fairly. It has been updated to explain the importance of first asking ‘Must We?’ and ‘Can We?’ to support compliance with our legal and regulatory obligations, before asking ‘Should We?’. > **[See our Code of Conduct at commbank.com.au][/p][olicies]**

## **Managing our business responsibly** Effective governance is essential for delivering our strategy and helps drive better outcomes for customers, shareholders and financial system stability. Since the 2018 APRA Prudential Inquiry we have focused on our governance, culture and accountability. We continue to strengthen policies, systems and processes to deliver improved outcomes for stakeholders. Given the significance of environmental, social and governance issues, the Board has responsibility for overseeing efforts to improve the experience and outcomes of CBA customers, monitoring our culture and considering the material environmental and social impacts of our activities. The Board oversees the Group’s Risk Management Framework (RMF) and approves the risk appetite statement (RAS), which embeds a culture focused on disciplined risk management. The Board also approves a range of key Group policies and frameworks. Some of these include the Remuneration Policy, Code of Conduct, Diversity Equity and Inclusion Policy, E&S Policy and Framework, and Work, Health and Safety policies. Our frameworks help embed our policies and procedures across the organisation. All employees undertake compulsory annual training relevant to their role. This supports business decisions and fairer customer and community outcomes. > **[For more information on our approach to corporate governance, see ][pages 34][–][57.]** > **[For more information on how we are managing our risks, see ][pages 58][–][67.]** **==> picture [9 x 533] intentionally omitted <==**

Our culture, policies, procedures and processes aim to support good customer outcomes. text: ## **Engaging with our regulators** We maintain transparent and constructive relationships with both financial and non-financial regulators to support strong and consistent outcomes for our customers and the broader community. CBA engages proactively with regulators to listen to feedback and respond in a timely manner to meet our regulatory engagement principles and obligations. Domestic financial regulators play an important role in maintaining the stability, fairness and efficiency of Australia’s financial system. A strong financial system protects consumers and contributes to the country’s prosperity. Trust and confidence in our financial system attracts investment in Australian banks, enabling us to lend to Australian households and businesses. Globally, bank deregulation has emerged as a significant topic. Domestically, there is increasing investor interest in the impact of regulation on housing affordability, access to credit, regional banking, and fraud and scams. Australia’s regulation has served our economy well through uncertain times. Financial regulators have a key role in considering regulatory reforms that could address domestic issues such as housing affordability and access to banking services. CBA aims to engage with regulators on key issues, and share our customer insights and other relevant perspectives.

## **Improving payments regulation** **Delivering a safe, reliable and efficient payments system is a regulatory priority. We welcomed the RBA review of merchant card payment costs and surcharging as an opportunity to deliver better outcomes for consumers and small businesses. Customer preferences towards contactless payments and ecommerce is growing with electronic payments being the lowest cost form of payment to accept for merchants.** **We recognise that it is in Australia’s national interest to have an Australian bank providing banking services in the Pacific, helping to promote social and economic integration. This year CBA committed to opening a banking agency in Nauru to provide limited transaction, savings and merchant services. CBA is working closely with the Australian Government and the Government of Nauru to deliver a smooth transition of services later this calendar year.** **It is important that payment regulation applies to popular payment solutions such as digital wallets and buy-now-pay-later services. To simplify the system, we support removing surcharging for both credit and debit cards with safeguards so that small businesses are supported and benefit from lower costs. With interchange fees supporting a range of benefits valued by customers and merchants, appropriate pricing and economics across the payments ecosystem is essential for a safe, reliable, sustainable and innovative payments system.** **The interaction between these policy changes and proposed legislative changes to the** _**Payment Systems (Regulation) Act 1998**_ **are important and complex. The RBA is consulting to ensure there are no unintended consequences and any changes are in the best interest of Australia’s payments ecosystem and end users.**

## **Meeting our regulatory obligations** Authority, after paying a $7.5 million fine for breaches of certain provisions of the _Spam Act 2003 (Spam Act)_ . We are committed to improving how we classify electronic customer messages and strengthening our systems, processes and controls to support ongoing compliance with the _Spam Act_ . To meet our regulatory obligations and deliver better customer outcomes, we have policies and procedures in place and track our obligations to our customers. This includes responsible lending obligations, which aim to encourage prudent lending and minimise the risk that retail customers will not be able to make their loan repayments. Retail customer-facing employees complete annual responsible lending training and assessments, where required by their role. We also periodically review, audit and assure our lending processes. ASIC’s Better Banking for Indigenous Consumers project included observations on the way banks, including CBA, can provide effective products and services to First Nations customers. In response, CBA committed to making discretionary payments to certain identified customers relating to certain fees dating back to July 2019. CBA has contacted the majority of eligible customers and made discretionary payments. CBA has engaged with ASIC regarding its response to ASIC’s project, including ASIC’s concerns regarding fees paid by a broader cohort of concession customers. Where we have not met our regulatory obligations, we seek to fully cooperate with regulatory investigations to remediate any harm and put things right. In October 2024 CBA entered into an amended Enforceable Undertaking with the Australian Communications and Media

## **Respecting human rights** Our E&S Framework sets out our minimum requirements through which we seek to manage the potential impacts of human rights in relation to the Bank’s operations, supplier management, and financing and bond facilitation. grievances to be raised via phone to our Indigenous Customer Assistance Line. The process seeks to provide an avenue for First Nations stakeholders to raise, directly with us, concerns regarding possible human rights impacts connected with CBA’s business lending activities. No grievances were raised through this process this financial year. During the year members of our Indigenous Advisory Council, Modern Slavery Advisory Council and Community Council provided important connection points to help inform our approach to key human rights issues. The Bank continues to monitor transactions. We use a library of red flags and typologies to identify potential money laundering, terrorism financing and other financial crime offences including flags for modern slavery and child exploitation. As part of our processes, we aim to identify human rights risks we consider to be relevant to our business activities. Our ESG risk assessment tool assists our bankers to identify and assess relevant human rights risks that our customers are exposed to as part of our commercial and corporate lending processes. > **[See our Modern Slavery and Human Trafficking statement ] at commbank.com.au/reporting** This year we expanded access to our Human Rights of First Nations Stakeholder Grievance Process by enabling **See our E&S Framework and Grievance Process Framework at commbank.com.au/policies**

## **Fostering a safe workplace** **==> picture [201 x 307] intentionally omitted <==** Our focus on the health, safety and wellbeing of our people helps them reach their full potential. It also reflects the right of all people to work in an environment that is free from unlawful workplace conduct, such as discrimination, harassment, sexual or sex-based harassment, bullying and victimisation. We have always taken our obligations to keep our people safe seriously and the positive duty for organisations is aligned to our approach. A range of key programs and processes help us maintain a safe workplace. This includes our ‘Respect Lives Here’ initiative and our health and safety management system. ‘Respect Lives Here’ is our prevention initiative focused on building a shared understanding of respectful and disrespectful behaviours at work. This year we again partnered with the University of New South Wales to survey all of our people, listen to their experiences, and provide practical guidance on becoming active bystanders when something does not feel right. As part of our prevention strategy, our education and training programs help people understand our expectations of appropriate workplace behaviour. This includes how to identify, report and address conduct-related issues. The Bank expects appropriate standards of conduct in accordance with our Code of Conduct at all times. We take appropriate disciplinary action in relation to any breaches of our Conduct Policy, the Code of Conduct or our values, up to and including dismissal from employment. **For more information on how we promote the health, safety and wellbeing of our people, see page 83.**

## **Speaking up** **We strive to create a work environment that promotes the right behaviours. Providing our SpeakUP services supports our people and external partners to raise concerns safely, including anonymously if desired. Support and protection are provided to whistleblowers under the Group Whistleblower Policy and applicable laws.** **The Audit Committee and an executive committee receive reporting on the operation of SpeakUP three times a year and quarterly, respectively. This year 408 reports were made to the SpeakUP Program, up from 331 in 2024. Of these reports, 68 were whistleblower disclosures.**

## **Advocating responsibly** CBA engages governments directly, as well as through our industry memberships in relation to public policies that impact banking and sustainability issues. Our approach to advocacy is focused on issues that may impact national long-term prosperity. Over the past year, we have engaged on the following policy areas: > **[Contributing to housing policy development]** - **[A whole-of-ecosystem approach to help reduce ] fraud and scams** - **[Australia’s transition to net zero in support ] of a whole-of-economy transition plan** - **[Fair competition in the payments system and ] investment in future payments infrastructure[Supporting regional banking services ]** - **[Responsible use of AI]** - **[Legislative reforms to provide additional cyber ] protections for Australian citizens and businesses** - **[A sustainable cash-in-transit sector and ] long-term access to cash**
## **Cyber security, privacy and data management** Improving customer trust in banking by keeping our systems running safely and protecting our customers.

## **Our approach to tax** **CBA is one of the largest taxpayers in Australia. We recognise the important contribution taxes make to support Government assets and services. Our approach to managing our tax affairs is in accordance with CBA’s values, purpose and strategy. Our commitment is to comply with prevailing tax laws in all jurisdictions that we operate in, and to maintain transparent and collaborative relationships with tax authorities.** > **[See our Tax Transparency Code at commbank.com.au/re][p][ortin][g]**

## **Position on political donations** **The Bank’s external communication and engagement policy prohibits political donations in the form of cash or money. We will pay to attend political events and forums. This year we spent $78,400 with the Australian Labor Party, $77,619 with the Liberal Party of Australia, and $18,500 with the National Party of Australia. These payments are disclosed to the Australian Electoral Commission in line with State and Federal regulation.** CBA has made a number of climate-related public commitments. These include supporting net zero by 2050 as part of collective efforts to limit global temperature rises. We have supported the development of a sustainable finance taxonomy and welcomed development of sectoral pathways, as well as supported the implementation of mandatory climate-related financial disclosures. These public commitments align with the Australian Banking Association and Business Council of Australia positions. CBA is a member of the Australian Sustainable Finance Institute, where we have contributed to its Taxonomy Technical Expert Group. We are also a member of the Green Building Council of Australia, which is focused on leading the sustainable transformation of the built environment, and the Electric Vehicle Council, which aims to increase certainty for investment through policy. **==> picture [179 x 105] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Working with our suppliers** Suppliers are important partners in delivering our strategy and managing our risks. We contract with over 3,100 Australian suppliers, including over 1,600 Australian small businesses. Indigenous-owned suppliers are providing products and services to the Bank and this year we spent over $62 million with Indigenous suppliers, up 177% compared to FY24. As part of our FY26-28 RAP, we are aiming to spend a cumulative $100 million with First Nations businesses over the next three years, with a focus on introducing new suppliers where practical.

## **Related material topics** - **Cyber security and resilience** - **Data security and management** - **Financial crime** - **Fraud and scams** - **Privacy** > **[Refer to materiality on ][p][a][g][es 72–73. ]**

## **Most relevant risks** - **Artificial intelligence** - **Business disruption and technology** - **Cyber security** - **Financial crime compliance** - **Financial risk** - **Fraud and scams** - **Privacy and data management[Refer to risk on ][p][a][g][es 65–67.]**

## **Improving customer trust in banking** Banking is an essential service for customers, who depend on having secure and reliable access to cash and payment systems. CBA has a role to play in protecting our customers and contributing to financial system resilience. We understand the importance of continued investment and resources to keep our systems resilient, minimise disruption and protect customer data. However, as cyber threats grow more sophisticated and frequent, the risks to our customers, communities and operations continue to evolve. We are committed to helping protect our customers and the broader community from fraud, scams, cyber threats and financial crime. Doing so requires a whole-of-ecosystem approach. We are committed to working with governments, regulators, banks and other industries to support a national response.

## **Vigilance on cyber security** Cyber resilience and information security remain key priorities for the Bank. As cyber threats become more frequent and complex, we continue to invest in strategies, advanced technologies such as AI and GenAI, and skilled teams to help protect our customers, assets and data. This year we enhanced the resilience of our cloud infrastructure and improved key cyber control operations. For example, we implemented near real-time code scanning to help detect and mitigate risks associated with sensitive information in our code. We are adopting AI tools to help detect and neutralise external threats more efficiently. We also worked with our suppliers to enhance their data and system security, helping to further strengthen our own resilience. To help support system-wide resilience and strengthen the national security ecosystem, we engage closely with Government and industry. Alongside industry partners, we contributed to a consultation process that led to the introduction of Australia’s first standalone cyber security law – the _Cyber Security Act 2024._ We also collaborated with the Tech Council of Australia and the Group of Eight Australian Universities on the inaugural Australian Cyber Exchange 2025, which aimed to showcase and strengthen Australia’s sovereign cyber security capabilities. We continue to strengthen our cyber resilience by regularly reviewing and testing our approach, as well as engaging external firms to assess and provide feedback. We look to integrate insights from these assessments into our risk mitigation strategies to help enhance our protective and defensive capabilities. We consider cyber security a shared responsibility across the Bank. Our people play a key role by helping build secure processes and products, and effectively identifying and responding to cyber threats. We have built a large and capable security team of approximately 1,400 people and actively support developing the next generation of cyber talent. > **[For more information on how we manage cyber security risk, ] see pages 64–65.**

## **Safeguarding customer privacy** We have a responsibility to protect the personal information of our customers. We apply processes and controls to respect and protect our customers’ personal information, aiming to prevent data breaches and responsibly govern personal information in accordance with our internal privacy policy. Our public Group Privacy Statement provides transparency on how the Bank collects and handles personal information, in compliance with privacy laws. Following the enactment of the _Privacy Act 1988_ reforms in December 2024, we are working to update our Group Privacy Statement to provide greater transparency on how we use personal information for our automated decision-making processes, including the types of personal information used. We continue to enhance our personal information management processes through periodic reviews of our RMF, and updates to internal policies and standards. For suppliers who collect or handle customer personal information, we have processes to assess whether their data and privacy governance, policies and incident response measures are in line with our responsibilities. Recognising the ever-evolving challenges of safeguarding personal information, we are committed to meeting our regulatory requirements, with customer and community expectations in mind. > **[See our Group Privacy Statement at ][commbank.com.au/privacy]** > **[For more information on how we manage privacy risk, see ][p][a][g][e 65.]** **==> picture [166 x 272] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Keeping our customers safe** **Keeping our customers safe is a priority. This year we commenced rollout of multi-factor authentication (MFA) as an added layer of protection against unauthorised access to customers’ accounts and to keep their money safe. We began our phased rollout of MFA in April 2025 to our NetBank registered customers who are also CommBank app registered. Once enrolled, each time a customer logs into online banking, they will need to confirm the login attempt through our CommBank app.**

## **+$900 million** **1,400 of our people dedicated to security** **invested this year to help protect our customers against fraud, scams, cyber threats and financial crime** **==> picture [221 x 196] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Modernising our data infrastructure** Protecting and serving our customers begins with how we manage data – one of our most valuable and differentiating assets. Access to good quality data means we can make better decisions faster, mitigate risks, and deliver more innovative and personalised customer experiences. It also serves as a key input in our AI solutions. Our ambition is to make it easier for our people to securely access data faster, enabling them to unlock greater value from data. This year we have made progress modernising our data technology and used AI to reduce complexity and duplication in our data.

## **Combatting financial crime** As a major financial institution, we play a key role in combatting financial crime to help protect the integrity of the financial system, our customers and communities. We continue to invest in detection and case management capabilities to better assess risk across customers, channels and products, while strengthening our AML/CTF compliance to meet regulatory obligations in Australia and other jurisdictions. To support identification and management of risk, we systematically review guidance from regulators, intergovernmental bodies such as the Financial Action Task Force, and non-government resources to understand and address emerging financial crime trends and typologies.

## **Raising scam awareness** **Money mule scams are an increasing form of financial crime in Australia, particularly targeting students and young people. This year CBA partnered with media company Campus Group to raise awareness on the scams across 13 university campuses nationwide. The campaign focused on educating students about the risks and consequences of mule scams, helping them recognise and avoid potential threats.** Alongside industry partners, we continue to contribute to the Fintel Alliance’s efforts to combat money laundering, terrorism financing and other serious crimes. This year we worked with AUSTRAC and other major banks to analyse 56 million data points under $10,000, uncovering criminal patterns that would be difficult for individual institutions to detect alone. To better protect our community from financial crime, we introduced QR Cardless functionality in the CommBank app to enable secure, card-free ATM transactions. This feature eliminates shared credentials, verifies identity for every transaction, and uses behavioural and geolocation analytics to detect suspicious activity.

## **Faster financial crime assessments using AI in the Business Bank** **We are actively exploring how AI can support our teams in combating financial crime. This year we deployed an AI-driven solution to accelerate early detection and response in financial crime risk assessment. The model enhances prioritisation of potential cases in the Business Bank, enabling analysts to concentrate on high-risk threats. Initial deployments of the model have demonstrated an improvement in detection, strengthening our analytical capabilities, and enhancing protection for customers and the broader community. This initiative reflects our commitment to innovation and safeguarding stakeholder trust.**

text: ## **Related material topics** - **Artificial intelligence** - **Digital innovation** Banking is becoming increasingly digital, and stakeholders expect innovation that delivers secure, personalised and seamless experiences. We are strengthening our digital capabilities by modernising our technology and data platforms, embedding AI and analytics into our core services, and investing in scalable infrastructure to support operational resilience. - **Digitisation[Refer to materiality on ][pages 72][–][73][.]**

## **Most relevant risks** Our ambition is to responsibly harness data and emerging technologies to better understand customer needs and deliver superior digital experiences. We empower our people with advanced tools and insights, and enable them to focus on what matters most – supporting customers with seamless, personalised banking experiences. We continue to attract and retain top talent in AI and engineering. We also remain committed to responsible AI practices that drive safety and trust as we scale AI capabilities across the Bank. - **Artificial intelligence** - **Business disruption and technology** - **Cyber security** - **Financial crime compliance** - **Financial risk** - **Fraud and scams** > **[For more information on how we use data, AI and technology to deliver safe and exceptional ] customer experiences, see pages 20–23.** **• Privacy and data management[Refer to risk on ][p][a][g][es 65–67.]**

## **Accelerating innovation with AI Factory** **We recently launched the AI Factory, our platform for safely testing, developing, and scaling advanced AI models on our proprietary data. Built on Amazon Web Services (AWS) latest infrastructure, it enables our teams to train and fine-tune AI models faster and more efficiently. The AI Factory helps support increased scale, performance and sophistication in GenAI use cases by addressing Australian language and banking nuances. We can now process data at an unprecedented scale enabling us to run a deep learning model over 3 trillion data points across 4 billion transactions. Generating one million data points is 50% faster and requires 90% less compute time because of our transition from Central Processing Units (CPUs) to Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). GPU-based models can transcribe approximately 100,000 call centre interactions in 15 hours, a task that would have previously taken three times as long.** > **[Refer to strategy on ][pages 16][–][25][.]** **==> picture [9 x 533] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Transforming banking with responsible AI** **==> picture [166 x 295] intentionally omitted <==** The adoption of AI can offer customers an enhanced banking experience, but we recognise the risks associated with the use of AI. Our responsible approach to AI focuses on managing these risks, while seeking to maximise customer benefits. We have developed responsible AI principles. These guide how we apply our existing risk management framework and policies to design, develop, deploy and manage AI across the Bank. Our responsible AI toolkits provide model owners and developers with clear, practical guidance to assess model performance, test for bias, and help to enable fairer and consistent customer outcomes. This year we enhanced our generative responsible AI toolkit to better assess model performance across areas like accuracy, fairness, reliability and privacy. We have also introduced a guide to help our developers identify the types of problems that are best solved using GenAI. To promote safer customer interactions with our GenAI solutions, we implemented technical guardrails designed to detect harmful content, sensitive data and jailbreaking attempts. We continue to establish partnerships that help us strengthen our approach to responsible and human-centred AI development. This year we collaborated with MIT to understand how we can enhance our AI-powered products, refine risk practices and advance AI advocacy. The collaboration begins with two research projects focused on establishing best-practice AI risk mitigation strategies and designing AI-powered tools that enable better human and AI collaboration. We also expanded our strategic partnership with Anthropic and held a three part education series to upskill over 2,300 of our people on agentic coding and responsible AI practices. **==> picture [96 x 37] intentionally omitted <==** **----- Start of picture text -----**

We continue to engage with the Federal Government in shaping AI regulation in Australia. This year we provided feedback on their proposed mandatory AI guardrails. We also engaged over 30 community organisations through our Community Council in meaningful dialogue about our AI journey and approach, while also listening to their concerns and perspectives on AI. **==> picture [144 x 30] intentionally omitted <==** **----- Start of picture text -----**

We regularly review our responsible AI approach, to keep pace with evolving technology, regulations and best practices. As the AI landscape continues to shift, we expect our approach to evolve accordingly.

## **Environmental impacts from AI** **AI has the potential to enhance customer experiences by making products and services more personalised and easier to use. As digitisation accelerates, the demand for electricity will continue to grow. It is important to recognise and address the environmental impacts of AI, particularly related to energy and water use. While we purchase the equivalent of 100% renewable electricity for our Australian operations, which include our Australian data centres within our operational control, much of our AI compute capacity is provided by third-party providers.** **We also seek to minimise water impacts in our operations and report annually on water usage in our commercial and data centre operations. We are continuing to work with key suppliers to better understand the climate-related impacts of services they provide to us to gain a more precise and comprehensive picture of our carbon footprint, including with our providers of AI services.** **==> picture [6 x 203] intentionally omitted <==** **----- Start of picture text -----**

## **Message from our Chair and CEO** Australia’s transition to a net zero economy by 2050 is underway. Government policies, and new generation and transmission infrastructure are assisting. As the bank for all Australians, we remain committed to helping our customers and supporting Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050. Meeting Australia’s 2030 interim emissions reduction target requires significant investment. Estimates suggest Australia’s transition to net zero needs more than $600 billion of investment by 2050 to decarbonise the nation’s industry and energy systems. CBA can support our customers to fund their transition. Energy security is crucial to the success of the Australian economy. Australia is facing a critical moment in the energy transition, needing to deliver important national energy infrastructure that lowers emissions quickly and affordably. Limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels appears increasingly difficult and the pathway to net zero, globally, is looking narrower. The Australian Government is continuing to develop a national Net Zero Plan to guide our country’s transition to meet our legislated target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. The energy sector continues to be the biggest contributor to Australia’s domestic emissions. We believe that affordably decarbonising Australia’s electricity grid remains the most important step for Australia. **Australia’s future economy needs more affordable and reliable energy** Historically, Australia has been a reliable energy producer and exporter, making affordable energy prices a competitive advantage. As we transition to a net zero economy, we need to maintain this advantage to support Australian living standards and help build a brighter future for all. The demand for electricity in Australia is increasing due to economic and population growth, increased digitisation and electrification. Access to affordable and reliable energy sources is needed to support Australia’s prosperity and future economy. While progress on meeting Australia’s renewable energy target is commendable, over reliance on one energy source can lead to vulnerabilities in our electricity markets, blackouts and increased costs, putting more pressure on energy bills. We welcome the Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) work on approaches to grid stability. All energy sources and grid stability approaches have trade-offs such as emissions intensity, cost, time-to build and impacts on nature. We see an important role for governments and industries to balance and communicate those trade-offs and develop sound policies. Building community support for Australia’s transition to net zero is important. We welcome policies that can help Australia deliver more affordable and reliable energy for all Australians, now and into the future.

## **Balancing trade-offs to support the transition** Australia needs effective climate change policies that reduce emissions, provide investment certainty, support economic growth, and minimise increased costs for essential goods such as food and electricity. Expanding renewables in Australia’s electricity grid has been challenging due to insufficient transmission infrastructure and complex planning processes across different levels of government. AEMO has modelled that Australia can meet its renewable target provided planned investments are delivered, making critical energy infrastructure a national priority. Policy coordination is also needed to better integrate consumer energy resources into the grid, benefitting the system and all consumers. Grid reliability risks include extreme weather, energy shortfalls and operational issues with ageing coal-fired power generators facing early closure. Government and national energy bodies have signalled gas will remain a key part of Australia’s energy mix during the transition. This is a pragmatic trade-off, as gas currently remains critical for key industrial processes, as well as serving as a secure and reliable back-up to renewables. We note the Government is currently undertaking the Gas Market Review to consider the effectiveness of the current framework to, amongst other things, ensure there is sufficient domestic supply. Balancing environmental and economic outcomes, while increasing renewable energy and maintaining grid stability, is needed.

## **Continuing to support our customers** Given one in three Australians and one in four Australian businesses call us their main financial institution, we play an important role in financing economic activity. However, the main driver of emissions reductions for our retail and small business customers is Australia’s electricity grid transitioning. We continue to provide lending products and tools that can help our customers understand the actions they can take to reduce their emissions, make their homes and businesses more energy efficient and aim to ease cost-of-living pressures. Harder-to-abate sectors, such as transport, agriculture and heavy industry are important sectors for Australia’s future economy and need balanced, long-term support to transition. While these sectors make up a smaller portion of our lending, compared to housing, our aim is to continue working with our customers in these sectors and exploring ways we can help them reduce their environmental impact.

## **Supporting Australia’s energy transition** Affordably decarbonising Australia’s electricity grid is essential for Australia’s economy. As Australia’s economy and population grows, households and businesses electrify, and digitisation increases, the demand for electricity will continue to grow. A reliable and affordable electricity grid is integral to the economy and Australia’s future prosperity. Electricity accounts for around 34% of Australia’s emissions. Decarbonising the electricity grid is critical to the decarbonisation of other sectors, including housing – the largest sector that CBA finances. For Australia, and the Bank, to achieve its emissions reduction ambitions, the electricity grid needs to decarbonise. Replacing coal-fired power stations with renewables is challenging. The nation needs to address long planning timeframes, supply chain constraints and increase community support for infrastructure. Installing rooftop solar remains popular with consumers. The Government’s renewable energy target provided Australia with direction. Recent policies including the Capacity Investment Scheme and Rewiring the Nation are helping to accelerate the transition. With generation capacity and transmission infrastructure progressing, Australia is better placed to meet its 2030 target of a 43% reduction in emissions below 2005 levels. It is our understanding that Australia should be able to produce sufficient generation to meet growing demand over the next decade, provided current State and Federal Government projects to build renewable and dispatchable generation, transmission assets and policies to coordinate consumer energy resources eventuate. Ongoing monitoring, policy adjustments and managing new challenges are essential for helping Australia remain on track. Achieving Australia’s emissions targets and producing reliable, affordable energy requires effective community engagement and policies that seek to maintain our country’s energy advantage. **==> picture [10 x 842] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Maintaining system reliability and stability** Renewable energy generation is increasing. However, high electricity costs remain a concern for consumers and businesses. Australia needs to find affordable ways to achieve its 2030 renewable energy target and maintain system stability. We continue to support AEMO’s view that flexible gas-powered generation is crucial in a high renewable electricity system. Along with batteries and pumped hydro, gas can provide critical backup to variable renewable energy, reliability as coal-fired power stations retire, and flexibility to adapt to demand changes. Gas plants, capable of rapid startup, help to provide continuous electricity supply and support grid reliability and stability, especially during high-demand periods and extreme weather. Australians broadly support a focus on the nation’s climate change ambitions but are concerned about the impact on their cost of living and quality of life. The transition requires government and industry to balance and communicate competing trade-offs between energy sources. Effective system management and grid stability will continue to be important to maximise use of renewables while preventing potential blackouts.

## **Reducing emissions in key sectors** Australia’s Climate Change Authority (CCA) has published six sector pathways.[ 1] The CCA’s report identifies potential technologies and actions for each sector that, taken together, could deliver net zero emissions for Australia by 2050. The CCA recognises that emissions must fall across all sectors, however each sector is on a different pathway to net zero by 2050. For some sectors, like power generation, with coordinated planning, the pathway may be steep and rapid as technologies are mature and ready to scale. Sectors like agriculture, however, are expected to experience a slower and more gradual path as technologies are in early development. Government policy support and investment are needed to accelerate the deployment of early-stage technologies and actions. The table below includes key sectors[ 2] informed by the Bank’s sector-level financed emissions. ## **Our role in helping to build Australia’s future economy** Since 2009 we have progressively reduced the emissions from our operations, for example the energy that powers our branches and buildings. This now makes up less than 1% of our total emissions. However, the emissions associated with the lending we provide to our customers is more than 99% of our total emissions. Importantly, much of the emissions produced by our customers and suppliers come from activities or actions that are not within the Bank’s direct control or are more challenging to influence. Climate change can have a significant impact on the Australian economy and our communities. Given one in three Australians and one in four Australian businesses call us their main financial institution, our role is to help build Australia’s future economy by supporting our customers and communities as they navigate the choices they need to make to transition to a lower-carbon economy. While climate change is not currently estimated to be financially material to the Bank in the short term, it is important that our climate strategy aligns to our purpose. This means supporting our customers as they take action to adapt to and/or mitigate the physical or transition impacts of climate change. Further, the risks we may be exposed to or the opportunities that may be available to us need to be assessed, quantified where possible, and have an appropriate level of control and oversight by management and the Board. We acknowledge encouraging behavioural shifts or action on climate change can be challenging, take time and requires trust. As we approach 2030 our focus will be on working with our customers and suppliers to help them understand the actions they can take to transition and build their resilience to climate impacts. > **[For important information on how we have assessed the materiality of climate change, see ][pages 70][–][73][.]** > **[For important information on how we have assessed the resilience of our business model, see ][pages 149][–][158][.]**

text: ## **Building resilience and supporting an inclusive transition** small businesses. Insurance affordability and underinsurance is already a risk to our customers and is an emerging risk to the Bank. While we continue to offer emergency assistance and tailored support options to our customers and communities, we acknowledge that our efforts have been focused on short-term, post-event support. We are supportive of government assistance that considers long-term outcomes, investment in climate-resilient infrastructure and home retrofitting programs. Australia is making progress in transitioning to net zero. However we acknowledge certain stakeholders may be disproportionately impacted. This includes businesses and households who may struggle to switch to loweremissions technologies and regions impacted by changes in employment opportunities. These challenges can be amplified by the physical impacts of climate change. Lower-income households, renters and apartment residents may find it more difficult to participate in the home energy transition due to costs, split incentives or practical infrastructure challenges. We are supportive of State and/or Federal Government policies that consider an inclusive transition and address the needs of more vulnerable communities. We are building our data and analytical capabilities to better understand the impact of climate on our customers. This year we launched the Natural Hazard feature pilot in the CommBank app using the New South Wales (NSW) Rural Fire Service’s bushfire dataset. The pilot enables customers to understand whether their property may be located on bushfire prone land to support their adaptation and mitigation actions. Increasingly frequent and severe weather events are impacting insurance affordability, intensifying cost-of-living pressures for homeowners and reducing the resilience of - 1 ASB is subject to a separate New Zealand mandatory disclosure regime and expects to publish a standalone climate report later this year. text: ## **Strategy** Our purpose is to build a brighter future for all, inspiring us to support Australia’s transition to a more prosperous, resilient and sustainable future. Our climate strategy aims to deliver on our purpose. **==> picture [10 x 842] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Supporting Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050** In helping build Australia’s future economy, our climate-related opportunities are centred on supporting our customers to transition to a lower-carbon economy and in helping them make their homes, businesses or activities more resilient to the impacts of climate change. We also aim to continue assessing, managing and monitoring our climate-related risks, and investing in our direct operations to reduce our environmental impact. While the financial impacts of climate change for CBA may be less immediate and significant when compared to other material issues, we have developed initiatives which aim to address climate-related risks and opportunities. Our climate strategy includes mitigation and adaptation actions. Current opportunities include: developing specific banking products and services to support customers to reduce their emissions and finance their transition or adaptation initiatives; supporting customers with natural disaster recovery; helping customers to assess their climate risks and develop adaptation strategies; and collaborating with stakeholders to develop tools, insights and research that can be shared. We set our first operational emissions targets in 2009. To further support our climate strategy, in 2022 we set our first sector-level financed emissions targets. We take meeting our commitments seriously and are pleased to have met our 2025 Scope 1 and 2, and Scope 3 operational emissions reductions targets. We are also below the reference scenario for 12 of our sector-level financed emissions goals and targets. **For important information on how we identify climate-related risks and opportunities, see pages 154–158.** **==> picture [515 x 64] intentionally omitted <==** **----- Start of picture text -----**

## **Lending to support the transition** continued This year we have taken the opportunity to clarify how we classify our aspirations as goals or targets. This resulted in some previously reported targets now being described as goals, supporting our continuous efforts to enhance the accuracy and transparency of our reporting. This change is intended to better align to where our pathways for achieving outcomes are subject to key external dependencies, for example the pace of Australia’s energy transition. We have set 10 goals and five targets covering 71% of CBA’s in-scope drawn lending. For several of these sectors, including Australian housing, Australian commercial property and aluminium, lower emissions are heavily reliant on grid decarbonisation. Should the electricity grid not decarbonise at the expected rate, or if State or Federal Government policy settings do not support decarbonisation, then achieving our goals for these sectors will be made more challenging. We continue to identify actions we can take to support our customers.

## **Actions we are taking** Many factors can influence our financed emissions, including the composition of our lending portfolio, and our customers’ greenhouse gas emissions and activities. As we work towards our 2030 goals and targets, our reported figures may fluctuate up or down. Our approach to setting and achieving our goals and targets may also evolve as new data, methodologies and other factors emerge. Importantly, we do not expect our customers to follow the specific sector-level pathways we are working towards.

## **How to read our sector-level charts** There are five key concepts to understand our sector-level financed emissions progress. - **1 Baseline:** reflects our portfolio’s starting point in terms of absolute emissions or emissions intensity. - **2 Actual:** our portfolio’s financed absolute emissions or emissions intensity for a given financial year. - **3 Reference scenario:** the science-based scenario we currently use to inform our goal or target and what we compare our portfolio’s financed absolute emissions or emissions intensity to. We expect to review these over time.

## **There are three ways we are working towards our sector-level financed emissions goals and targets:** - **4 CBA portfolio:** an assessment of how the portfolio’s financed absolute emissions or emissions intensity estimate for the current reporting period compares to the reference scenario at the same point in time. - **5 Goal or target:** our financed absolute emissions or emissions intensity goal or target for the portfolio to be achieved by 2030.

text: ## **Taking steps that can help our customers reduce their emissions** For some sectors the charts do not include the baseline or actual to protect our customers’ confidentiality. This is to support cases where, for example, only one customer has drawn lending in the reporting period. Our approach varies by sector but can include engaging with customers, providing insights, data and dedicated products, services and tools, as well as advocating for government policies that can help them reduce their emissions. For some sectors, our baseline absolute emissions or emissions intensity is not the same as the reference scenario base year. For example, where our portfolio is not representative of the relevant Australian or global sector, to account for the impacts of COVID-19 on the sector, or due to data limitations.

text: ## **Supporting our retail and business customers** There is a role we can play in helping our customers better understand their climate impact and make more informed choices as part of the transition to a lower-carbon economy.

## **Helping our retail customers** Australian consumers are increasingly investing in their own energy transitions with the installation of rooftop solar panels, battery storage and purchase of EVs. However, the costs to implement these technologies continues to be a barrier for many Australians who are seeking energy bill relief or fuel savings. Our approach is to help guide our customers by raising awareness of the technologies available, providing education, connecting customers with installers and EV manufacturers, and providing financing options and offers. With one in four Australian businesses naming CBA as their main financial institution, we aim to continue supporting small-to-medium businesses. We have a range of sustainable funding solutions to support our business customers to reduce their emissions, help our customers save on costs, build resilience and capture new growth opportunities. We offer tools which can help our customers identify opportunities to make sustainable business changes. Our Green Buildings Tool can help customers with commercial property identify actions which may improve energy efficiency and reduce emissions in their buildings. The tool estimates the upfront costs of implementing these actions, potential reduction in electricity costs upon implementation and the potential impact on the building’s National Australian Built Environment Rating System (NABERS) energy rating. Our Sustainability Action Tool offers insights, actions and resources to help small-tomedium businesses reduce environmental impacts and business costs, focusing on energy, transport and waste. Our Home Energy Upgrades service is designed to support customers through every step of their home energy upgrade journey, to help inform their decision making and understand potential energy bill savings. The service also connects customers with accredited solar and battery installers across Australia offering personalised quotes, along with discounted finance options and special offers. Our Home Energy Assessment Tool, developed in collaboration with Home Efficiency Australia, helps educate our customers by providing them an efficiency score and a cost-benefit breakdown for different home energy upgrades. To help simplify the car purchasing process for our customers we developed the Buy and Own a Car platform, enabling customers to purchase cars, including diesel, petrol and EVs. The platform encourages EV uptake by offering customers EV and charger discounts, an EV cost comparison tool, discounted finance, and educational resources to buy new and used cars. To support eligible essential workers and those earning under $100,000 per year, we launched the EV Access Program in partnership with the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (CEFC). This program offers lower-cost finance options for EVs under $55,000 enabling more customers to experience fuel savings through EVs. To better assist our customers with their sustainability journeys, we support our bankers with further learning, development and educational opportunities. This year Business Banking (BB) partnered with the Australian Graduate School of Management to deliver a ‘Future focused banking’ program. The program was completed by more than 150 of our approximately 800 frontline business bankers. It focused on improving banker knowledge and skills to discuss the opportunities and risks of the transition to a lower-carbon economy with our customers.

## **Supporting our large corporate and institutional customers to transition** We intend to support our large corporate and institutional banking customers in line with our credit policies, E&S Framework commitments, and sector-level financed emissions goals and targets. Our larger customers are generally more progressed on transitioning or adapting their businesses to make them more climate resilient. Our approach is focused on working with our customers to understand their long-term transition plans and funding needs. We provide financing solutions where it may assist their plans.

text: ## **Banking products, tools and services** We offer a range of financing solutions to support our customers in achieving their climate strategies and goals. We have a full range of financial markets capabilities, capital raising solutions, transaction banking services, and risk management products and services. Our sustainable finance team is dedicated to supporting customers in taking actions that drive better E&S outcomes, for example by linking their sustainability strategy to their financing arrangements. This includes structuring and facilitating use of proceeds instruments. Our carbon team also provides bespoke solutions to support project developers with managing price risk in the carbon market and supporting businesses to acquire or provide Australian Carbon Credit Units (ACCUs).

## **Engaging our institutional customers on their transition readiness** Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) framework and undertaking additional climate stress testing. This is expected to increase with the introduction of mandatory climate reporting in Australia. ## **Lending in line with our E&S Framework** The E&S Framework outlines our minimum requirements that seek to manage the climate impacts of our financing activities, including bond facilitation. This includes requirements for certain clients in the fossil fuel sectors, which can help us work towards our 2030 financed emissions targets for thermal coal mining, upstream oil and gas extraction and power generation. As set out in the E&S Framework, these requirements are subject to Australia having a secure energy platform. **See our refreshed 2025 E&S Framework at commbank.com.au/policies**

metadata.section: **Lending in line with our E&S Framework**

text: ## **Client Transition Plan assessments and criteria** In 2023 we clarified our expectations for certain clients to have a Transition Plan from 2025. This year this expectation applied to existing oil and/or gas producing or metallurgical coal mining clients who derive 15% or more of their revenue from the sale of oil, gas or metallurgical coal; or power generation clients who generate 25% or more of their electricity from coal, and to who we offer corporate or trade finance, or bond facilitation. We continued to engage a third party to independently assess applicable clients’ Transition Plans against the requirements set out in our E&S Framework, using the core criteria set out below. Unless we had already determined we would cease to offer new corporate or trade finance, or bond facilitation to a client from 1 January 2025, we continued to monitor the Transition Plans of applicable clients in FY25. In some instances, we determined the client would not have, or would be unlikely to have, a Transition Plan meeting our core criteria by 31 December 2024. After making this determination, we did not provide new corporate or trade finance, or bond facilitation with a maturity beyond 31 December 2024, except for uncommitted exposures that could be cancelled by 31 December 2024. After 1 January 2025, we did not provide new corporate or trade finance, or bond facilitation to clients whose Transition Plans did not meet the core criteria, based on the third-party assessment. We took the same approach for refinancing. Otherwise, existing exposures for these clients remain on our balance sheet beyond 31 December 2024 until their maturity. From the publication of our 2025 E&S Framework, our Transition Plan expectations will also apply to clients who derive 25% or more of their revenue from the sale of thermal coal, where we provide corporate or trade finance, or bond facilitation. **See our refreshed 2025 E&S Framework at commbank.com.au/policies**

## **Sector overview and outlook** As at 30 June 2024, Australian housing accounted for 63.9% of our in-scope drawn lending. Residential buildings in Australia use approximately 24% of overall electricity and contribute over 10% of total carbon emissions.[ 2] Home emissions are mainly driven by electricity and gas for heating or cooling, cooking and hot water. While many households have made home energy upgrades, further work by industry and government is required to support homeowners in apartments and townhouses where energy efficiency measures are more difficult to adopt.

## **Our goal and portfolio** As at 30 June 2024, the emissions intensity of our portfolio was 35.0 kgCO2-e/m[2] , a reduction of 3.8 kgCO2-e/m[2] compared to our 2021 baseline, 0.1 kgCO2-e/m[2] compared to June 2023 and is 17% above the reference scenario. The modest reduction compared to 2023 partly reflects a change in the data provider we use to calculate a home’s floorspace and number of bedrooms, and limitations in using publicly available data sets. Our financed emissions calculation draws on publicly available household energy consumption benchmarks meaning, at times, it is unable to account for the impact of increased solar and battery installations or changing energy usage by our customers. > **[For important detail on the governance and monitoring of our Australian housing financed emissions goal, see ][page][ 14][0][.]**
