## **Dependencies and challenges** The reference scenarios that inform our goals assume the decarbonisation of Australia’s electricity grid, the uptake of distributed energy resources, construction of more energy efficient buildings, and building owners making operational improvements and/or retrofitting their buildings. State or Federal Government policies that support electrification and improved energy efficiency in new or existing buildings would also support achievement of our goals. In addition to the pace of grid decarbonisation, sector disruption in the form of rising construction costs and low construction labour availability may slow the transition and impact our ability to achieve our goals.

## **Sector overview and outlook** As at 30 June 2024, lending to the Australian commercial property sector accounted for 6.9% of our in-scope drawn lending and 3.3% of our financed emissions. In Australia, commercial buildings use approximately 25% of overall electricity and contribute 10% of total carbon emissions.[ 2] Newer commercial properties tend to be more energy efficient and are expected to be better positioned for the transition, while older buildings need significant capital expenditure and upgrades to improve their energy efficiency.

## **Our goals and portfolio** As at 30 June 2024, our 2030 goals cover 77%[ 3] of our in-scope drawn lending to the Australian commercial property sector and include the office, retail and industrial sub-sectors. We have set separate goals for these sub-sectors to recognise the different baseline emissions intensities for different types of buildings. This year we have changed our goals to reflect a material refresh of the Government’s Commercial Building Baseline Study (CBBS). Key changes in our goals for the retail and industrial sub-sectors are largely driven by reallocation of energy demand across building types in the 2024 CBBS as compared to the 2022 CBBS. Therefore our industrial sub-sector progress, which was above the reference scenario last year, is now below the reference scenario. It also means, we are unable to report year-on-year progress for these sub-sectors as the CBBS update does not provide comparative information. As at 30 June 2024, the emissions intensities of our office, retail and industrial portfolios were 58.1 kgCO2-e/m[2] , 48.6 kgCO2-e/m[2] and 30.8 kgCO2-e/m[2] , respectively. This is below the reference scenario for all portfolios, reflecting differences in our portfolio’s composition compared to the national average. > **[For important detail on the governance and monitoring of our Australian commercial property goals, see ][p][a][g][e 14][0][.]**

text: ## **Sector overview and outlook** We define the heavy industry sector as the production of steel, alumina, aluminium and cement. As at 30 June 2024, lending to the heavy industry sector represented <0.1% of our in-scope drawn lending and 13.3% of our financed emissions. In 2023, Scope 1 emissions from the production of alumina, aluminium, iron, steel, lime, cement and other metals accounted for approximately 7% of Australia’s total emissions.2 Greenhouse gas emissions from heavy industry production generally occur from the high heat and chemical reactions required in manufacturing processes. These industries are also significant electricity consumers. Steel is essential for many other sectors, such as construction and machinery, and is expected to continue playing an important role in Australia’s energy transition, including the construction of wind turbines and solar farms. Cement is required for housing, buildings and infrastructure. Alumina is an intermediate product in the production of aluminium, which is used in technologies that are also critical for reducing emissions. Heavy industry is considered harder-to-abate due to its reliance on grid decarbonisation, process efficiencies and low-emissions technologies that, in many instances, are not yet commercially viable at scale in Australia.

## **Our goals and portfolio** Our heavy industry portfolio is concentrated to a small number of companies. To protect our customers’ confidentiality, we have adopted a ‘traffic light’ disclosure of our portfolio against goals. This is to support cases where, for example, only one customer has drawn lending in the reporting period. Portfolio is between ≥0% and ≤10% above the reference scenario. ## **Sector overview and outlook** As at 30 June 2024, lending to the power generation sector represented only 0.5% of our in-scope drawn lending and 1.9% of our financed emissions. In 2023, Scope 1 emissions from the power generation sector accounted for approximately 34% of Australia’s total emissions.1 Retiring coal-fired power stations and shifting to renewable sources of energy is critical to reducing the emissions intensity of Australia’s electricity grid. Renewable electricity can provide a cost-effective way of reducing emissions for consumers and is not only essential for the nation to meet its decarbonisation ambitions, but also to support Australian households and other sectors in reducing their emissions. In the 2024 Integrated System Plan (ISP), AEMO’s step change scenario projects that up to 90% of the National Energy Market’s coal-fired power stations will retire by 2035 with the remaining 10% retiring by 2040. Renewable energy connected with transmission and distribution, firmed with storage and backed up by gas-powered generation, is the lowest-cost way to supply electricity to homes and businesses as Australia transitions to a net zero economy.2

## **Our target, portfolio and progress** Our interim 2030 target is 105 kgCO2/MWh which is a 53% reduction compared to a 2020 baseline. As at 30 June 2024, the emissions intensity of our portfolio was 91 kgCO2/MWh, a reduction of 131 kgCO2/MWh compared to our 2020 baseline and 33 kgCO2/MWh compared to 30 June 2023. Our portfolio was also 73% below the reference scenario. The reduction in our portfolio emissions intensity was primarily driven by lower exposures to non-renewable power generation customers, new drawn lending to the renewables sector and changes in customer emissions. While the emissions intensity of our portfolio has continued to decrease since June 2020, drawdowns of unused lending limits could change our share of customers’ emissions and generation resulting in potential fluctuations in emissions intensity. Our power generation portfolio is diversified by technology and geography with over 50% of our lending exposures outside Australia. Our power generation portfolio is also 72% weighted to lending to solar and wind generation assets, 13% to other renewable generation assets, along with smaller drawn exposures to electricity generators and gentailers that are more emissions-intensive. > **[For important detail on the governance and monitoring of our power generation financed emissions target, see ][p][a][g][e 140.]**

text: ## **Assumptions and risks in achieving our target** The reference scenario that informs our target assumes a significant increase in renewable power generation from solar and wind, and a significant decrease in unabated fossil fuel generation by 2030. To maintain grid reliability and stability, and to reduce the sector’s emissions, investment in firming in the form of batteries, pumped hydro and some gas-fired electricity generation is crucial. We see a role for government policy and public funding to de-risk renewable energy and transmission projects. Should government policy settings change or not be implemented as currently stated, it may impact our ability to achieve our target.

## **Sector overview and outlook** As at 30 June 2024, lending to the upstream oil and gas extraction sectors represented <0.1% of our in-scope drawn lending and 1.9% of our financed emissions. In 2023, Scope 1 emissions from upstream oil and gas extraction accounted for approximately 10% of Australia’s total emissions.1 These industries also have significant downstream emissions due to the combustion of the products they produce. In AEMO’s 2024 ISP, as coal-fired power stations retire, gas-powered generation is expected to continue playing a role in supporting Australia’s economic activity through the transition. Gas-powered electricity generation can be used to provide firming support to variable renewable energy when other dispatchable sources are unavailable. Gas is also used in a range of industrial applications where lower carbon alternatives are not yet commercially available, particularly those requiring heat over 500°C. AEMO’s 2025 Gas Statement of Opportunities forecasts shortfall risks under peak conditions from 2028, three years later than forecast in 2024. AEMO’s update reinforces the need to complete committed and anticipated production, storage and infrastructure developments, amongst other measures.

## **Actions we are taking** We support customers in these sectors by providing lending in line with our E&S Framework. text: ## **Reviewing our operational emissions strategy and targets** This year we completed an evaluation of our operational emissions strategy as part of our five-year review cycle. The review considered our Scope 1 and 2, and Scope 3 reduction targets, boundaries and inventories, and incoming new mandatory climate reporting requirements. Given the significant progress in executing our reduction strategies for Scope 1 and 2, we are increasing our reduction target from 42% to 75% by 2030 against our 2020 baseline. We are also able to expand our Scope 1 and 2 target coverage from 2026 onwards as we now have better data for our other overseas offices, including India. We have also made several changes to improve how we measure, manage and represent Scope 3 operational emission sources, particularly those associated with our supply chain. Where we do not currently have activity data available, we are developing spend-based estimates. We have conservatively estimated our expanded footprint as an increase of approximately 600% from our reported 2024 operational emissions. As our current Scope 3 target accounts for only 13% of our expanded estimated emissions, the existing Scope 3 target is no longer meaningful in its present form. Accordingly, we will reassess this target and focus on more accurately quantifying our Scope 3 operational emissions in line with new mandatory climate reporting requirements in 2026.

metadata.section: **Reviewing our operational emissions strategy and targets**

text: ## **Supporting action outside our operations** In 2024, ASB pre-purchased carbon credits for 2025 sourced from GHG removal projects under the Permanent Forest Sink Initiative (PFSI). In 2024, Toitū Envirocare announced its commitment to align their practices with international standards. As a result, they will be moving towards no longer accepting carbon credits issued under the New Zealand PFSI for offsetting purposes. Toitū Envirocare honours the use of pre-purchased, ‘reserved’ New Zealand credits. As part of the transition phase, ASB will apply 2024 pre-purchased credits sourced from New Zealand-based PFSI compliant projects to maintain its Toitū Envirocare Net Carbon Zero certification. We do not use carbon credits to meet our operational emissions targets. However, we continue to support climate action beyond our value chain, such as purchasing carbon credits and investing to help reduce our travel emissions. This year CBA signed several multi-year agreements supporting improved social, cultural and environmental impacts through projects within the ACCU scheme. Our portfolio focuses on projects supporting Australia’s Indigenous communities and aligns with our Reconciliation Action Plan. This year CBA supported Indigenous savanna burning projects which also have benefits for nature. Selected projects went through a due diligence assessment, to assess the integrity and credibility of the carbon credits generated. This due diligence assessment was based on the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market’s Core Carbon Principles and transparency changes to the ACCU scheme. Given air travel emissions are particularly hard to reduce, CBA has been part of the Qantas SAF coalition for the past two years. The coalition aims to support the scaling of the SAF industry to reduce aviation emissions. During the year we increased our level of participation to become a ‘partner’, which contributes to the airline’s incremental cost of purchasing SAF. The use of SAF purchased through CBA’s partnership would be equivalent to avoiding 1,000 tCO₂-e of CBA’s air travel emissions. We continue to monitor developments related to the ACCU scheme and note the review Climate Active is currently undertaking. We will reassess our position as more information becomes available.

## **Actions to help us reduce our supply chain emissions** Air travel emissions represent 70% of the emissions in our current Scope 3 operational emissions target. Our efforts to date have been directed towards mitigating our own air travel impacts and supporting lower-carbon alternative fuels. Our Australian business monitors business travel and tracks actual emissions against internal carbon budgets to balance the demand for business critical travel while focusing on meeting our Scope 3 target. We also continue to take steps to reduce the impact of our office and branch fit-outs by making them more resource efficient. Our refurbishment projects incorporate sustainable design principles, and we look to reuse and repurpose existing building materials and furniture, wherever possible. Our three-year ATM refresh project, covering approximately 1,700 ATMs, is implementing a modular construction system using lower-carbon, natural and renewable materials. A circular design approach is being taken, facilitating efficient installation and easy disassembly for repairs and reuse. In addition, our latest container branch, designed to support communities after natural disasters, considers sustainable design principles. The container itself has been reused, and approximately 70% of its interior is fitted with lower-carbon and circular materials, such as wall linings made from upcycled packaging, recycled plastic acoustic panelling and furniture, as well as lower-carbon carpet and joinery panels. We also measure the impact of our offices via major projects aiming to achieve lower embodied carbon compared to previous comparable buildings in our portfolio. This year we completed the Bankwest Place refurbishment in Perth, achieving a 42% reduction in embodied carbon. This is compared to the estimated emissions for a typical fitout with conventional material selections.

text: ## **Understanding the impact of climate and nature issues on Australian agriculture** Australian agriculture is exposed to both climate- and nature-related risks and opportunities given the emissions created, carbon sequestered into land, and the impacts and dependencies to produce food and fibre for our economy.

metadata.section: **Understanding the impact of climate and nature issues on Australian agriculture**

text: ## **Continuing to support Australian agriculture** The Australian agriculture sector is essential for our economy and food security, and is central to regional communities and the financial health of their economies. The sector accounts for 18% of Australia’s net emissions, or 16% excluding land-use, land-use change and forestry. 1 Landowners face risks including acute weather events, a changing climate and loss of ecosystem services.

## **1.8%** **in-scope drawn lending** as at 30 June 2024 However, many are exploring options to reduce net emissions for improved profitability, enhancements to natural capital for production, and incentives in environmental markets and schemes. Availability and costs to implement new technologies, and balancing competing land uses in the agriculture industry, continue to slow the pace of progress on emissions reductions for the sector.

## **financed emissions** The Bank has been supporting the Australian agriculture sector for over 100 years, and we intend to continue supporting our farmers through our lending and other activities. We recognise that our customers are at different stages of adopting decarbonisation activities and responding to the transition. We partner with companies like Ruminati to provide our farming customers with complimentary tools to estimate their baseline emissions and develop tailored action plans to help them reduce their on-farm emissions. Our aim is to continue investing in research partnerships and programs to build our understanding and share insights with our customers. as at 30 June 2024

## **Key nature dependencies[ 2]** **Soil erosion** **Water availability Climate regulation Flood and storm protection** The agriculture sector faces specific challenges in goal and target setting, including measuring emissions, multiple gas sources, different agricultural activities, and the way emissions are generated and stored through natural systems. We continued to explore the possibility of setting financed emissions goals and targets for the Australian agriculture sector, which were deferred in 2024 due to data and methodology challenges. As these challenges remain unresolved, we have decided not to set goals or targets this year. We remain focused on helping customers measure their baseline emissions and have updated our methodology for measuring and reporting our financed emissions for the sector. **Water quality** **Key:[Very high ] High** **==> picture [483 x 133] intentionally omitted <==** 1 Refer to page 429 for source. 2 Based on our 2023 Exploring Natural Capital Opportunities, Risks and Exposure (ENCORE) analysis as published in our 2023 Climate Report.

## **Nature and biodiversity** We continue to recognise the interconnection between nature and climate issues, and the importance of Australia taking action to maintain, restore and enhance nature and biodiversity.

## **Progressing our approach to nature** With one in four Australian businesses calling us their main financial institution, we play an important role in financing economic activity. Sectors with greater exposure to nature-related risks, such as agriculture, mining and construction, are important to building Australia’s future economy and need balanced, long-term support to manage their impacts and dependencies.

## **Assessing naturerelated impacts in our own operations** As a large Australian lender to the housing and commercial property sectors, we believe we have a role to play in understanding the built environment’s impact and dependency on nature, starting with our own operations. Understanding our customers’ impacts and dependencies on nature can help us manage the risks and opportunities these create. Our 2023 ENCORE analysis identified agriculture and mining as priority sectors, as well as the built environment in relation to our operations. We continued to monitor our water and waste use which were identified as the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) metrics most material to our operations. As part of our ongoing efforts to reduce waste to landfill, we trialled reusable coffee cups, expanded the roll out of coffee cup sorting stations, upgraded our waste infrastructure and signage, and introduced a dry waste stream into our Sydney commercial offices this year. Since then, we have been building internal analytical capabilities, exploring emerging tools and piloting elements of the ‘LEAP’ (locate, evaluate, assess and prepare) framework. While data collection and measurement methods continue to evolve, there is a clear need for nationally consistent definitions, metrics and datasets tailored to the Australian context. We welcome the Australian Federal Government’s initiative to enhance environmental information through the newly established statutory body, Environment Information Australia. We continue to monitor developments under Australia’s Nature Positive Plan. We welcome further work across government and key industry stakeholder groups to develop nationally consistent tools and datasets that could support the pragmatic development of nature commitments and consider the interdependencies with climate objectives. As a continuation of our embodied carbon assessments, we engaged a third-party consultant to conduct an assessment into the impacts on nature from our retail fitout. The assessment identified the highest impact materials on nature as aluminium, steel and timber and further assessment of the supply chains of these materials were carried out. We continue to explore how these findings can be integrated into design decisions.

text: ## **Continuing to develop our measurement capabilities** We continued to build analytical capabilities to assess nature impacts and dependencies for parts of our lending portfolio. This includes taking opportunities to partner with organisations who can support better measurement of nature-related metrics and support customers in working towards improved nature outcomes. **==> picture [187 x 155] intentionally omitted <==** This year we built on previous geospatial analysis and continued to explore publicly available datasets and methodologies to assess where our operations and lending activities intersect with nature. This exercise identified challenges in timeliness and accuracy of publicly available information on the location of relevant assets. Through our climate stress test, we also explored exposure to water stress for select regions in our agriculture portfolio. We also participated in an Early Adopter Program with CSIRO to test their new NatureIQ tool that combines multiple CSIRO environmental indicators, models and datasets. The tool supports assessment and monitoring of indicators such as ecosystem condition and species extinction risk. **==> picture [10 x 842] intentionally omitted <==**
## **Governance** The Board continues to oversee the assessment of risks and opportunities for the Bank arising from climate change.

## **The Board’s oversight of climate issues** The Board’s responsibilities include considering the material E&S impacts of the Bank’s activities. Each of the Board’s four standing Committees assists the Board to carry out its responsibilities, with the Audit and Risk & Compliance Committees primarily assisting the Board with its oversight of climate issues. The Board approves the Group E&S Policy and Framework, and oversees the management of climate risk within the Bank’s overall business strategy and risk appetite. The Board also monitors the E&S work program, which includes the development and delivery of CBA’s climate strategy and progress against goals and targets. The Board and the Audit and Risk & Compliance Committees regularly receive reports from management on climate-related matters. text: ## **Executive remuneration** Our Executive performance and remuneration frameworks consider a variety of matters including climate. Executives’ remuneration outcomes are determined through the assessment of collective and individual measures, which include climate-related objectives where relevant as part of the ‘Strategy Execution’ key performance indicator (KPI) for short-term variable remuneration awards. For 2025, the ‘Strategy Execution’ KPI has a minimum weighting of 25%, for relevant Executives’ scorecards. While there is no set weighting for specific climate-related measures, execution and delivery of those climate-related measures will impact the overall outcome of the ‘Strategy Execution’ KPI. The Board can also exercise discretion to adjust individual and/or collective outcomes, including discretion to apply malus clawback provisions in the event of underperformance. As part of determining performance and remuneration outcomes, the four Board Committees met concurrently to review each Executive’s individual and collective accountability. For 2025, continued adherence to the E&S Framework has been incorporated into our risk and reputation modifier to maintain a strong link to remuneration outcomes. > **[For further information on executive remuneration, see ][pages][ 1][8][2–21][8][ of the ]** _**[Remuneration report]**_ **[.]** **Audit Committee** - At the August 2024 meeting , considered the 2024 Climate Report, including recommending the Climate Report to the Board for approval - At the August 2024 meeting, provided oversight of certain sector-level financed emissions targets, including recommending certain targets to the Board for approval - At the June 2025 Committee meeting, the Committee received an update on the implementation of mandatory sustainability reporting, including climate disclosures

## **Developing Board skills and continuing education programs** The Nominations Committee oversees the induction program offered to each new Non-Executive Director which is tailored to meet their needs. The induction program includes an overview of E&S issues as they relate to the Bank and our operations. The Committee also oversees the continuing education program provided to Directors. This year the Board continued to invest in E&S-related training with a session held on Australia’s energy transition. This was led by external experts and explored progress, challenges and opportunities in relation to Australia’s energy market. The Board assesses the appropriate mix of skills, experience, knowledge, independence, expertise and diversity required for effective governance, and the extent to which they are represented on the Board or relevant Committee. E&S is one of the skills included in the Board skills matrix which describes that a director understands potential risks and opportunities from an E&S perspective. text: ## **Management accountability** The Board has delegated the management of the Bank to the CEO, except for certain powers retained by the Board or delegated to others including Board and Management Committees. Once the Board has approved the strategic objectives and risk appetite of the Bank, which includes our climate strategy, the CEO is accountable for execution. The CEO then delegates authority to the Group Executives for the effective execution of the Bank’s operational activities. Responsibilities relating to the execution of our climate strategy and management of climate-related risks include:

## **Embedding climate governance within our business** Governance committees within the Bank, such as risk management committees, product governance forums and transaction-level committees, support the Board’s oversight and the Executive Leadership Team’s (ELT’s) management of climate-related risks and opportunities. Each of these committees and forums have charters that govern and outline roles and responsibilities. Climate-related financial risks and opportunities can be escalated through these reporting structures. Governance processes are supported by the application of a range of internal policies, standards and procedures that determine the way we deliver our products and services. For example, our Product Development and Distribution Standard embeds consideration of E&S product features into the product governance process, which includes oversight of changes to product features and periodic reviews through an E&S lens. Management of the Bank, including executing and delivering our strategy; and Chair of the Non-Financial Risk Committee (NFRC) and E&S Committee.

## **Chief Financial Officer** Reporting obligations, including our Annual Report; environmental policy settings captured in our E&S Policy; overseeing and reporting on our performance and progress towards goals and targets; executing our property strategy and managing the facilities in our Australia-based buildings; and management of our supplier framework, including relevant policies.

## **Chief Risk Officer** Creating and maintaining our risk appetite statement (RAS) and preparing the Board-approved RAS, including RAS indicators; ensuring an appropriate Risk Management Framework (RMF) is in place to manage our risks; ensuring appropriate processes and tools are in place to strengthen our risk culture; shares responsibility with business units for certain credit decisions[ 1] ; and Chair of the Financial Risk Committee (FRC).

## **Group Executives for Retail Banking Services (RBS), Business Banking (BB) and Institutional Banking and Markets (IB&M)** Products and services offered to our customers, which can include designing and distributing products or services with E&S features; shares responsibility with the Chief Risk Officer for certain credit decisions[ 2] ; creating and maintaining the RAS for their business unit; and ensuring the E&S Policy is adhered to in their business unit, including delivering actions and allocating resources in line with our commitments. Considering climate-related opportunities for the Bank is a responsibility for the Board and all employees, with individual opportunities predominantly identified by our customer-facing business units – RBS, BB and IB&M. Where appropriate, climate-related opportunities may be escalated to an appropriate management committee, or the Board, for consideration or approval. **==> picture [483 x 187] intentionally omitted <==**

text: ## **Transaction oversight for Institutional Banking and Markets customers** In RBS, we take a portfolio managed approach to E&S governance, implementing this for products, tools or features that we provide to customers, rather than through individual customer ESG risk assessments. For new CBA product offerings with E&S features, including the Home Energy Upgrades service, the Bank carefully considered the potential impacts to our conduct, strategic and credit risks. Before being sent, customer communications are reviewed to check environmental claims are accurate and can be supported. In IB&M, lending customers are relationship managed and supported directly by our bankers. As part of the corporate lending process, ESG risk assessments are completed for institutional customers, and are reviewed and refreshed annually. IB&M operates two key forums that support consideration of E&S risks and other reputational risks. These review forums, which involve senior management from within and outside IB&M, include an E&S Deal Review (EDR) and the IB&M Commitments Committee. Before credit approval, a proposed transaction is escalated to EDR if it meets certain conditions, including if the customer’s activities are captured in the relevant fossil fuel financingrelated commitments in our E&S Framework; the transaction may impact a sector-level target and/or exposure reporting for certain sectors; or the ESG risk assessment results in a heightened ESG risk rating. Where appropriate, the EDR can also escalate a proposed transaction to the IB&M Commitments Committee, particularly where it may impact the Bank’s non-financial risks, reputational risk, strategy or values. If the transaction is supported for approval, it then proceeds through the credit approval pathway.

Depending on the customer’s ESG risk profile, or where additional oversight is required, ESG risk assessments may be escalated to senior management or the BB Commitments Committee. text: ## **Risk** Climate-related risks can have different impacts on our customers, people, communities and the Bank. Our risk management approach helps us better understand and manage these impacts for the Bank. 143 142 CLIMATE DISCLOSURES

## **Our approach to climate-related risks and opportunities** Delivering our climate strategy requires an understanding of the different ways climate-related risks could impact our business, and how our business activities could impact the climate, our customers, people and communities. The Bank’s embedded RMF, culture and Code of Conduct, guide our people to manage climate-related risks and opportunities. Climate change has been identified as a risk that could have a material impact on stakeholders within our value chain and expose the Bank to both physical and transition risks. While our current analysis shows that climate change is unlikely to have material financial impacts on the Bank in the short term, failure to respond adequately to the potential and expected impacts of climate change could affect our long-term strategy, performance and franchise value. We acknowledge some of our customers, communities and regions will face greater climate impacts and risks than others, and we remain well positioned to support them. represents drivers of potentially material strategic, financial and non-financial risks to the Bank. We use a range of tools and techniques to help us identify, assess, manage and monitor climate-related risks holistically at the Group level, and on a portfolio basis or for individual customers in certain circumstances. This approach helps us explore the physical and transition risks from climate change that may impact our business and customers over different time horizons. It also helps us consider how our business activities can impact the environment, our customers and the community. We also perform transition and physical risk scenario analyses to evaluate the resilience of the Bank’s strategy and business model to climate-related changes, developments and uncertainties. Our climate scenario analysis, combined with our climate risk materiality assessment (CRMA), helps us understand our exposure to strategic, financial and non-financial risks from climate change, as well as our risks and opportunities over the short, medium and long term. We continue to enhance our climate risk management tools and practices in line with evolving industry practices, and regulatory expectations. The Bank manages risks, including climate-related risks, through our RMF. The RMF is reviewed by management, the Risk & Compliance Committee and the Board to accommodate changes in our operating environment, better practices, and regulatory and community expectations. Climate-related risks are embedded in the Board-approved risk taxonomy under our E&S risk type. E&S risk is integrated into the Bank’s governance structures, policies, risk appetite and strategic planning processes. text: ## **Where our climate-related risks and opportunities are concentrated** As a bank that provides deposit and lending services to Australian retail, business and institutional customers, our business and value chain may be exposed to climate-related risks and opportunities from a number of sources, including the customers and communities we support and serve. **==> picture [207 x 544] intentionally omitted <==**

text: ## **Strategic and reputational risk drivers** - Our commitment to support Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050 could be impacted by global economic and geopolitical changes. - Inadequate climate commitments or lending to companies facing reputational challenges could damage the Bank’s reputation and exclude us from opportunities in the global and domestic transition economy. - Obstacles in financing new industries could result in a competitive disadvantage and revenue decline in the long term.

## **Non-financial risk drivers** - Our branches, ATM network, payments processing infrastructure and the data centres we use could be impacted by extended outages from severe weather events. - Changes in our policies and practices to limit the Bank’s exposure to climate-related risks could result in the perception of unfair treatment to segments of customers. - Rapidly changing climate regulations could lead to compliance failures by the Bank or our suppliers, leading to penalties or legal action.

## **Financial risk drivers** - **Physical climate changes** – More frequent, severe weather events and long-term changes in climate patterns could cause damage or decline in asset values, impacting the ability of households and businesses to repay their loans. The severity of credit losses to the Bank may increase due to declining asset values held as collateral, especially for customers in high-risk areas without adequate insurance, or who are facing prolonged unemployment or business disruption. - **Climate transition** – New climate change or energy policies, technological advancements, or changing community expectations could reduce the business model viability of certain business or institutional customers. This could impact their ability to repay loans, with the severity of potential credit losses to the Bank increasing due to declining asset values held as collateral. Unemployment could also increase and home values could decline in regions dependent on these businesses, resulting in increased losses to the Bank from retail customers.

text: ## **How climate impacts credit risk** More frequent, severe weather events and long-term changes in climate patterns can cause damage or decline in asset values, impacting the ability of households and businesses to repay their loans. The ability of some businesses to repay loans could also be impacted by a decline in the viability of their business models and profitability. This could be due to new climate change and energy policies, technological advancements, or changing community expectations that impact demand for their products or services. Unemployment could also increase in regions dependent on these businesses, resulting in increased losses to the Bank from retail customers. Physical and transition factors could also decrease the value of the assets held as collateral by the Bank, resulting in more severe credit losses when a default occurs. It is important we assess and understand the impacts to help us manage our risks effectively.

text: ## **ESG Credit Standard** We have explicitly incorporated the consideration of ESG risk assessments into our credit risk framework through our ESG Credit Standard. The standard provides a structured framework for the way in which E&S risks are to be considered in credit risk assessment processes for our customers. Along with all our other group-wide credit standards, it establishes the minimum credit expectations and requirements for identifying, managing and monitoring a borrower or counterparty’s E&S risks. The standard, which is applicable across the Bank, requires that existing or new non-retail borrowers or counterparties that meet certain criteria be considered against the commitments in the Bank’s E&S Framework when performing a credit assessment. Throughout the credit process, E&S risks identified are assessed for their impact on our customers’ ability to repay. In some cases, the standard also requires reviewing the borrower’s collateral they pledge to the Bank for E&S risks. We have not currently identified a globally accepted, standardised methodology for quantifying climate-related impacts on credit risk. Therefore, our ESG credit assessments continue to be driven by customer due diligence and qualitative assessments in processes tailored to the risk of specific portfolios. We expect our approach to integrating ESG into our credit risk framework will continue to evolve and adapt as industry practices mature, and as regulatory and stakeholder expectations change.

## **Resilience of our business to climate change** Our climate scenario analysis, combined with our climate risk materiality assessment, helps us assess the resilience of the Bank’s business model and strategy to climate-related changes, developments and uncertainties.

The tool is supported by a set of inherent risk ratings across industry ANZSIC codes for nine key focus areas: climate and energy; climate physical risk; nature impact; nature dependency; human rights; labour rights and modern slavery; Indigenous rights; workplace health and safety; **Institutional Banking & Markets Number of lending assessments** 853 **completed[ 2] Number of assessments escalated** 29 **and noted at the E&S Committee**

## **Risk appetite statement** The Board-approved RAS defines the maximum risk allowable to deliver the Bank’s strategic priorities. Management is required to operate within risk appetite. We have integrated two quantitative RAS indicators to help minimise potential credit losses from portfolios with higher exposure to climate-related risks. These focus on physical risk in the retail portfolio and transition risk in the institutional portfolio. For home loans, our indicator measures the percentage of loans with high loan-to-value ratios and exposure to climate physical risks like floods, fires and cyclones. This helps monitor the likelihood of higher credit losses if property values fall in areas experiencing extreme weather. For institutional lending, the indicator tracks the percentage of loans to customers with high climate transition risk. This assesses the potential for and anti-corruption and governance. The tool also includes specific questions aimed at assessing whether lending to a customer is aligned to the commitments in our E&S Framework. The tool directs bankers to obtain appropriate business and credit risk approvals. Decisions on lending transactions may be escalated to senior management or business unit governance committees if the assessment requires further review against the E&S Framework or other ESG risk indicators. These escalation pathways support our bankers to make risk-based decisions that consider potential ESG issues. For relevant project-related finance transactions we follow the Equator Principles process requirements. ## **Climate scenario analysis** Climate-related risk is highly uncertain. We perform scenario analysis, as needed, to understand the potential future impacts of climate-related risks on our financial position, performance, cash flows and business model. It may also help us make decisions to manage our risks which may include updates to policies, changes to risk appetite settings, portfolio limits or exclusions and consideration in capital planning. We acknowledge some of our customers, communities and regions will face greater climate impacts and risks than others, and we remain well positioned to support them.

## **How we prioritise the scenarios we run** up-to-date reference point for exploring how climate change, climate policy and technological trends could unfold under different futures. We use a combination of scenarios to explore the impact of individual severe physical and transition events that could impact the Bank in any given year, as well as long-term climate scenarios to understand impacts to the Bank under different futures exposed to high transition or physical risks. The NGFS scenarios incorporate the latest climate science findings, recent economic and climate data, country-level policy commitments to reach net zero emissions, and the latest trends in renewable energy and mitigation technologies.

## **Long-term scenarios** This year we performed three long-term climate scenarios based on the NGFS scenarios. They explore futures with high transition risk (net zero 2050), higher transition risk (delayed transition) and higher physical risk (current policies). To date, global progress against the goals of the Paris Agreement has lagged, increasing risk of the net zero 2050 scenario being out of reach. The delayed transition and current policies scenarios were selected as the Bank believes slower global progress in climate policy increases the probability of either scenario occurring. ## **Outcomes of our long-term scenarios** Outcomes under all three long-term scenarios indicate the Bank’s business model remains resilient, and reinforces our approach to supporting Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050 and building climate resilience. While severe weather may cause substantial losses in some years in the long term, the financial impacts of climate-related risks are not currently considered material to the Bank. This is based on modelling which shows minimal impact on loan impairment expenses and average operating profit over time.

## **[Net zero 2050 and delayed transition]** impact to Australia is minimised by high levels of renewables penetration in the Australian electricity grid at that stage. The introduction of strong climate policies, immediately under net zero 2050, and after 2030 under a delayed transition, are assumed to increase production costs and reduce demand for emissions-intensive industries such as coal and gas mining, manufacturing and livestock farming. This results in a drag on the economy and leads to moderate increases in unemployment, which are felt more immediately under the net zero 2050 scenario. However, the net zero 2050 future requires less aggressive government policies allowing the economy to more gradually transition away from emissions-intensive industries over a longer timeframe. The cash rate is assumed to remain low under these scenarios, supporting sustained growth in house prices. This limits average credit losses for the Bank due to the continued strong average loan-to-value ratio of borrowers. However, some industries and regions are more impacted than others under these higher transition risk scenarios, such as mining, utilities, manufacturing and agriculture, and regional areas exposed to coal and gas extraction industries. The net zero 2050 scenario has the better outcome for the Bank in the long term as the orderly nature of the transition results in higher growth and lower credit losses. The delayed transition scenario has slower growth between 2035 to 2045 due to the disorderly nature of the transition before recovering. The economic impacts are relatively mild under both scenarios because declines in coal and gas exports are assumed to be partially offset by increased demand for Australia’s critical minerals. text: ## **Why we ran this scenario** Research indicates that large, populated areas across South-East QLD and Northern NSW may experience more severe cyclones in the future as cyclones begin to track further south. We ran this scenario to enhance our understanding of the potential losses to the Bank from an extreme weather event that may become increasingly plausible over time.

## **Key scenario assumptions** The scenario assumes two severe cyclones (Category 4) make landfall over South-East QLD a year apart. First over the Sunshine Coast and then Brisbane. Each of these Category 4 cyclones are currently individually assessed as 1-in-200-year events, however the probability of two severe cyclone events in successive years in this location is currently extremely low. This scenario results in significant property damage from wind, storm surges and inland cyclone-induced flooding. This is exacerbated where properties are not built to withstand Category 4 cyclone winds. Limited government support is assumed. Supply chain disruptions and downtime impact business productivity. Following the back-to-back cyclones, property prices decline in impacted areas and the events lead to an economic decline in QLD with unemployment rates increasing materially, particularly in regional areas.

Losses are approximately double in the retail portfolio compared to non-retail. Mortgage losses are driven by borrower repayment stress after accounting for insurance, coupled with property price declines in impacted areas. ## **Our climate risk materiality assessment approach** The CRMA describes the current and anticipated effects of climate-related risks and opportunities on the resilience of the Bank’s strategy, business model and value chain. **5x5 risk matrix** – Our risk matrix, updated in 2025, considers the impact and expected frequency of a risk eventuating, resulting in risks being rated as either low, moderate, medium, high or very high risk. Impact and frequency are assessed using the following: The CRMA assesses how current and anticipated climate-related risks and opportunities arising from each of the futures outlined in our long-term scenarios, may impact the Bank’s material risk types, strategy, business model and value chain across the current, short, medium and long term. The assessment of impacts to our material non-financial and strategic risk types was performed through workshops with senior management and risk type owners, including ASB. The assessment of financial risk impacts incorporated outcomes from both the long-term and acute scenarios performed this year: - **Expected frequency** ranges from ‘1 event every 10 years’ to ‘Multiple events in the next year’; and - **Impacts** uses a combination of qualitative factors and financial measures. Qualitative factors consider impacts on customers, our operations and people, shareholders, communities, and regulatory and legal. The quantitative financial impacts range from negligible ≤$1 million; minor >$1 million; major >$5 million; significant >$25 million; or critical >$100 million. - **The long-term scenarios** provided a perspective on impact trends that climate change could have over time on the broader economy, certain industry sectors and the Bank. - **The acute event scenarios** enabled us to assess the ability of the Bank to withstand severe, yet plausible, events that could occur in any given year under these futures. For example, a medium risk rating could arise from an event expected to occur once every 10 years, with a significant financial impact of $25 million to $100 million. Alternatively, a medium risk rating could also arise from multiple events expected to occur in the next year, but with a minor impact of $1 million to $5 million. The anticipated effects on the Bank under these scenarios were considered across four time horizons: - Current term (within the next 12 months). - Short term (~3 years) to align with the Bank’s strategic planning cycle. Each risk was assessed based on its impact to the Bank in the time horizon in which the relevant scenario occurs, rather than cumulative impacts over all time horizons. When assessing impacts for future time horizons under these scenarios, no additional material changes to the business model or control environment were assumed beyond those already in place. For example, while a potential strategic shift could mitigate some risks in the future, such changes were not factored into the future risk ratings. - Medium term (~10 years) to align with the timeframe of when physical impacts begin to diverge for the low versus high warming futures. - Long term (~30 years) to align with the Bank’s home loan portfolio where home loans

such changes were not factored into the future risk ratings. - Medium term (~10 years) to align with the timeframe of when physical impacts begin to diverge for the low versus high warming futures. - Long term (~30 years) to align with the Bank’s home loan portfolio where home loans can be contractually agreed to for up to 30 years. The risk ratings indicate the impact of climate change on the relevant risk type under each scenario. For financial risks and capital adequacy risk, ratings were determined with reference to the relevant Board approved RAS. For non-financial, E&S and AI risks our 5x5 risk matrix was applied. We acknowledge that available data and techniques to perform this type of assessment are still maturing across the industry. As a result, our assessment of the impacts of climate-related risks involves a greater reliance on assumptions than is typically required for more mature risk types, where historical data is a better predictor of future events. As data and assessment techniques improve over time, we anticipate that our future CRMAs will incorporate more advanced assessment techniques. **Risk appetite statement** – Risk ratings were set based on the expected position relative to the relevant Board approved RAS thresholds. For example, a financial impact resulting in the Bank being outside risk appetite would be rated as ‘very high risk’. **For information on our long-term and acute scenarios, see pages 150–151 and 152–153, respectively.**

text: ## **Anticipated impacts on our financial statements** In some years, the Bank may experience increases in credit losses due to extreme weather events, however the scenario results indicate that financial impacts to the Bank from climate-related impacts are not expected to be material. This reflects the nature of our operations, the sectors in which we operate, and our existing risk management frameworks and portfolio diversification, which together provide a degree of resilience against potential climate-related impacts. The Bank is well placed to identify and pursue available opportunities arising from Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050. For example, the development of sustainable finance products, tools and services to support customers to transition and adapt to the impacts of climate change. While climate change presents challenges to the Australian economy and our communities, our core business remains resilient. A relatively small proportion of the Group’s TCE is currently exposed to high or very high physical or transition risk. Our customers have historically demonstrated strong repayment performance and we have established support mechanisms to assist them in times of financial stress, including those potentially arising from climate-related events. Although severe climate-related events could result in an increase in single year credit losses, these losses are assessed as a medium risk to the Bank as they would not result in a breach of our current capital, liquidity or profitability RAS indicators. This reflects our strong provisioning levels and capital position. **For further details on our credit risk, see Note 9.2 on page 311 in the** _**Financial report**_ **.** **==> picture [483 x 384] intentionally omitted <==**

## **Climate stress index for agriculture** In May 2024, we launched the climate stress index (CSI) tool for our bankers, developed in collaboration with CSIRO. The CSI tool forecasts climate stress through to 2030 by postcode, based on key agri-climatic productivity variables across grain, livestock and dairy sectors. It provides a composite score for each postcode-commodity combination indicating whether climate stress is expected to decrease, remain stable, or increase moderately or at a high rate. The tool enhances our understanding of the degree, nature and location of chronic climate risks to our lending securities. Currently, 19% of the Bank’s relevant agricultural exposures are secured by properties located in postcodes with forecasted increasing rates of climate stress. The tool enables our bankers to have conversations with customers on their long-term climate adaptation plans relevant for credit risk assessment. CSI insights are also used for portfolio monitoring in livestock, grain and dairy commodities, helping us track exposure trends and inform strategic planning. Insights from the tool can be shared with customers through a Climate Insight Report, tailored to their region and commodities, to help them consider the data and plan for future climate-related resilience. We will retire our productivity mapping tool given the launch of the CSI which provides a forward view of climate risk. We will continue to assess tools and capabilities for our agriculture customers’ climate risk assessments.

## **Supplier risk governance tool** In June 2023 we introduced the environmental risk assessment in the supplier risk governance (SRG) tool. As part of CBA’s annual review, industry environmental risk ratings are updated to support the inherent environmental risk assessment of our suppliers. For suppliers in industries with high risk ratings, assessments are undertaken when onboarding for new services, or variation or renewal of an existing service, and form part of supplier risk screening before contracts are executed. In 2024, in addition to the assessments that were completed when onboarding suppliers in high-risk industries, we triggered the environmental risk assessment for our leasing agents and landlords, and our top 100 suppliers by spend. As a result, the number of suppliers assessed decreased from last year and now totals 71. Of these suppliers, all reported they had no regulatory environmental breaches over the past three years. **Based on the 71 suppliers assessed in 2025, we have been able to gain the following insights:** **83% 76% 61%** have documented are working to set and monitor environmental reduce their negative commitments and/ environmental impacts, for GHGs or policies in place for example, climate and nature impacts **80%** set and monitor are either using or reduction targets purchasing the equivalent for GHGs renewable electricity to cover a portion of their electricity needs

## **Financed emissions portfolio analysis** Our calculations cover 96% of our in-scope drawn lending exposure. Movements in the overall absolute financed emissions and emissions intensity of our in-scope drawn lending portfolio are generally dependent on changes in our portfolio mix over time and differences in emissions profiles at the sector or customer level. We estimate our 2024 absolute financed emissions for our in-scope lending portfolio at 22.6 MtCO2-e, an increase of 9% (+1.8 MtCO2-e), compared to the restated 2023 absolute financed emissions estimate (20.8 MtCO2-e). Most notable increases were observed in the transport and storage, and manufacturing sectors. These movements were partly offset by reductions in estimated absolute emissions in the mining sector. Decarbonisation of the grid, reflected in changes in grid intensity factors in our estimates, continued to contribute to emissions decreases in Australian housing and Australian commercial property.[ 1]

## **MtCO2-e 2.1** Changes in estimated customer emissions have contributed to a decrease from some sectors including mining, Australian housing and Australian commercial property. This was partially offset by increases in the manufacturing sector. Portfolio changes have contributed to an increase in financed emissions. This was largely driven by portfolio changes in the transport and storage, manufacturing, and agriculture, forestry and fishing sectors. This was partly offset by portfolio changes to the mining sector. Changes in estimated emissions can include changes in our customers’ reported emissions or reported activity, as well as changes in estimated emissions as a result of updated activity and economic emissions factors. Changes to our portfolio can include changes in our drawn lending exposure to new and existing customers, as well as changes in existing customers’ enterprise value, which result in changes to the share of these customers’ attributable emissions.

## **Reconciliation of Group total committed exposures to lending used for financed emissions calculations** emissions over our in-scope assessed portfolio, covering drawn lending of $860.5 billion. The in-scope drawn lending portfolio assessed represents 62% of total TCE. In-scope drawn lending refers to the on-balance sheet exposure to the sectors included within the scope of our financed emissions calculations. Some asset classes and sectors we lend to are currently excluded due to lack of available data, methodologies and/or relevance. text: ## **Capital deployment** Capital deployment relating to climate-related risks and opportunities may be categorised into the following: **Financing:** Climate-related financing refers to the offering of lending products, credit facilities, or other financing solutions that support customers in addressing their climate-related risks or pursuing their climate-related opportunities. Our SFT monitors the level of cumulative funding within the scope of our SFT eligibility criteria. **Investment:** Climate-related investment refers to capital deployed through financial instruments or equity stakes in public or private markets that relate to the Bank’s climate-related risks or opportunities and where climate considerations form a material part of the investment rationale or potential outcomes. This year CBA invested $46 million in climate-related investments. **Expenditure:** Climate-related expenditure refers to capital or operational spending incurred in managing climate-related risks or pursuing climate-related opportunities. This includes direct costs related to internal systems, infrastructure, tools or processes that are focused on climate risk mitigation, adaptation or resilience. No material direct climate-related expenditure was noted this year. Indirect costs include ongoing expenditure which would be incurred ordinarily, making it impractical to allocate costs as specifically climate-related. These indirect costs include activities such as branch and office refurbishments where we are actively incorporating sustainable practices through branch design and energy efficient retrofits; the ATM refresh project which incorporates lower carbon, natural and renewable materials; and the resourcing costs associated with ESG teams who work to deliver our climate strategy.

## **Internal carbon price** The Bank does not currently apply or use an internal carbon price. - 1 Reported as green property finance in CBA’s 2024 Climate Report. - 2 Prior period contributions have not been restated for changes in methodology. - 3 New and incremental financing since 1 July 2024 has been included in the scope of PwC’s limited assurance engagement, except for energy efficient residential buildings, as no new or incremental contributions have been added in FY25. - 4 As we consider the evolving market and sustainable finance initiatives, including the recent release of the Australian Sustainable Finance Taxonomy by ASFI, we have continued to omit new and incremental funding of this asset class’ contribution towards our SFT and will revisit our criteria next year. - 5 Prior to FY24, this was reported as a single asset class, ‘Social assets’.

## **Directors’ report** The Directors of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia present their report, together with the Financial report of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) and of the Group, being CBA and its controlled entities, for the year ended 30 June 2025.

## **Assets and liabilities** **Home loans** increased $43 billion or 6%, reflecting our continued focus on retaining existing customers in a highly competitive market as well as ongoing investment in our proprietary channel. **Business and corporate loans** increased $22 billion or 8%, driven by growth in business banking reflecting diversified lending across a number of industries as well as institutional and structured lending portfolios. **Deposits** increased $55 billion or 6%, primarily driven by continued growth in savings and investment deposits reflecting greater customer demand for higher yielding deposits.

## **Principal activities** We serve more than 18 million customers with a focus on providing retail and commercial banking services predominantly in Australia, and in New Zealand through our subsidiary ASB. Our products and services are provided through our divisions, Retail Banking Services, Business Banking, Institutional Banking and Markets, and ASB New Zealand. > **[A review of the divisional operations and their results for the financial year ended 30 June 2025 can be found on ][p][a][g][es 32–33.]**

## **Operating and financial review** The Operating and financial review section includes the information below as well as the information in the _Overview_ section on pages 2–13, _Creating value for our stakeholders_ section on pages 14–67 and _Financial performance_ section on pages 26–33.

## **Group profit** The Group’s statutory net profit after tax for the financial year ended 30 June 2025 was $10,116 million, an increase of $722 million or 8% on the prior year. Statutory net profit after tax from continuing operations for the financial year ended 30 June 2025 was $10,133 million, an increase of $652 million or 7% on the prior year. The increase was driven by a 5% growth in total operating income and a 9% reduction in loan impairment expense, partly offset by a 5% increase in operating expenses. Statutory net profit after tax complies with the requirements of the _Corporations Act 2001_ (Cth), Australian Accounting Standards and International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Cash net profit after tax is management’s preferred measure of the Group’s financial performance. It excludes items that are non-recurring in nature and are not considered representative of the Group’s ongoing financial performance (non-cash items). We use the cash net profit after tax to present a clear and consistent view of our financial performance from period to period. The Group’s cash net profit after tax including discontinued operations for the year ended 30 June 2025 was $10,253 million, an increase of $406 million or 4% on the prior year. Excluding discontinued operations, cash net profit after tax for the year ended 30 June 2025 was $10,252 million, an increase of $416 million or 4% on the prior year. For further detail on the drivers of cash net profit after tax, refer to the _Financial performance_ section on pages 26–33.

## **Litigation and regulatory matters** A number of litigation proceedings against the Group are continuing. The proceedings include the defence of seven class actions. These include two separate shareholder class action proceedings (the appeal judgment was delivered in May 2025), two class actions in relation to superannuation products, two class actions related to financial advice (one of which was dismissed in May 2025, but has been appealed), as well as a class action commenced in New Zealand against ASB Bank regarding disclosure of loan variations. There are a range of ongoing matters where domestic or foreign regulators or other bodies are investigating whether CBA, ASB Bank or another Group entity has breached laws or regulatory or other obligations. Where a breach has occurred, or obligations have not been met, regulators or other bodies may impose, or apply to a Court for, fines and/or other sanctions, or may require remediation. The subject matter of these investigations is wide-ranging, and include a number of historical issues, which were notified to, or identified by, regulators or other bodies. The Group is also party to one enforceable undertaking and one compliance program with a regulator and continues to receive various notices and requests for information from its regulators, particularly in Australia and New Zealand, as part of both industry-wide and Group-specific reviews. In addition to regulatory investigations, enforcement actions, fines and other financial penalties, there may also be financial exposure to claims by customers, third parties and shareholders and this could include further class actions, customer remediation or claims for compensation or other remedies. The outcomes and total costs associated with such matters, and possible claims, individually or collectively, remain uncertain. The Board continues to monitor significant proceedings and investigations. The Group also continues to engage with its regulators and other bodies in relation to the matters under investigation and review. > **[For further information about some of the more significant litigation and regulatory matters referred to above, refer to Note 7.1 in the ]** _**[Financial ] report**_ **on pages 289–292.** 179 178 Directors’ report (continued)

## **Change in state of affairs** On 5 March 2025, the Group announced that it had completed the sale of its remaining 4.4% shareholding in Vietnam International Commercial Joint Stock Bank (VIB) via the Ho Chi Minh Stock Exchange. On 10 June 2025, the Group announced the completion of the sale of its remaining 5.45% shareholding in Bank of Hangzhou Co., Ltd (HZB) to New China Life Insurance Co., Ltd (NCI), a Beijing headquartered life insurance company dual listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange and the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. Changes to the Board are outlined in the _Our approach to corporate governance_ section on pages 34–57. > **[For further details, refer to Note 1.1 and Note 11.3 in the ]** _**[Financial report ]**_ **[on ][pages][ 22][9][ and ][359][, respectively.]**

## **Events subsequent to reporting date** The Directors have determined a fully franked final dividend of 260 cents per share amounting to $4,351 million. CBA expects the Dividend Reinvestment Plan for the final dividend for the year ended 30 June 2025 will be satisfied in full by an on-market purchase of shares of approximately $790 million. On 13 August 2025, CBA announced a 12-month extension of the on-market share buy-back of up to $1 billion of CBA ordinary shares originally announced on 9 August 2023 (of which $282 million was completed during the year ended 30 June 2024 and $18 million was completed during the year ended 30 June 2025). The Bank reserves the right to vary, suspend or terminate the buy-back at any time. The Directors are not aware of any other matter or circumstance that has occurred since 30 June 2025, that has significantly affected or may significantly affect the operations of the Group, the results of those operations or the state of affairs of the Group in subsequent financial years.

## **Environmental reporting** We are subject to the Federal Government’s National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting (NGER) scheme. The scheme makes it mandatory for controlling corporations to report annually on greenhouse gas emissions, energy production and energy consumption, if they exceed certain threshold levels. Our NGER submission is independently audited and submitted before the deadline to ensure that the Group meets the NGER requirements. We do not believe that we are subject to any other significant environmental reporting regulations under the law of the Commonwealth or of a State or Territory of Australia. - **[For more information on our voluntary environmental reporting, see the ]** _**[Climate disclosures]**_ **[ section on ][p][a][g][es 100–173 and our ]** _**[Social and ] governance performance metrics**_ **section on pages 94–99.**

## **Modern slavery reporting** We published our 2024 Modern Slavery and Human Trafficking Statement (Statement) in December 2024. The Statement outlines the actions taken by CBA Group to assess and address modern slavery and human trafficking risks in our business operations and supply chain, over the financial year ended 30 June 2024. This Statement was prepared in response to the reporting requirements of both the _Modern Slavery Act 2018_ (Cth) and the _Modern Slavery Act 2015_ (UK). We remain focused on this critical issue and will continue to report in line with the _Modern Slavery Act_ requirements. > **[For further detail on our disclosures, refer to our Modern Slavery and Human Trafficking Statement at commbank.com.au][/][sustainabilit][y][re][p][ortin][g]**

text: ## **Other changes to remuneration arrangements** Technology is a critical enabler of CBA’s strategic priorities. Gavin Munroe (Group Chief Information Officer) was granted a one-off award comprising of $1.50m of 9,681 performance rights to recognise his responsibility for delivery of agreed technology priorities over a three-year period. These priorities are designed to support the modernisation of CBA’s technology estate; strengthen technology leadership; enable greater stability, security, and continuity; enable the utilisation of new tools, technologies and AI; and enhance customer experience. Performance measures underpinning the award include: - Transition of technology to a security-first framework across CBA; - Delivery of agreed technology execution priorities; and - Model deployment, standards and technology requirements for AI across business lines, and acceleration of software development times. The vesting outcome will be determined by the Board in 2027 and 2028 through an objective assessment of the performance measures that reflect the successful delivery of key outcomes in CBA’s technology strategy agenda. Each performance right entitles Gavin to receive one CBA share, subject to vesting conditions. The number of performance rights that vest following the performance assessment could range from 0% to 100%. The performance rights do not receive dividends (or dividend-equivalent payments). ## **People & Remuneration Committee and Board oversight** The People & Remuneration Committee is the governing body for developing, monitoring and assessing the remuneration strategy and framework across CBA on behalf of the Board, ensuring that these are aligned to regulatory requirements, appropriate and operating as intended. The role of the People & Remuneration Committee is to review, challenge, assess and, as appropriate, endorse the recommendations made by management for Board approval. The Board reviews, challenges, applies judgement and, as appropriate, approves the People & Remuneration Committee’s recommendations. The People & Remuneration Committee met formally eight times during the 2025 financial year with the following members (as at 30 June 2025): Simon Moutter (Chair), Lyn Cobley, Paul O’Malley and Mary Padbury. The responsibilities of the People & Remuneration Committee are outlined in its Charter, which is reviewed annually.

## **The Charter is available at commbank.com.au/peopleandremuneration** As part of the performance and risk review, and to support the determination of remuneration outcomes for the CEO and Group Executives, the People & Remuneration Committee meets concurrently with the Risk & Compliance, Audit, and Nominations Committees. These concurrent meetings provide an opportunity for the Committees to review and recommend relevant risk and audit matters that may warrant consideration in the People & Remuneration Committee’s determination of remuneration outcomes. Information provided to the concurrent meetings supports the review and recommendation of collective and/or individual remuneration arrangements, including outcomes and variable remuneration adjustments. Considerations at the meeting include risk scorecard outcomes for the CEO and Group Executives, details of material risk matters presented by the Group CRO and outcomes of internal audit reviews conducted during the year, presented by the Group Auditor. The concurrent meeting process is structured to support the determination of appropriate remuneration outcomes and meet regulatory requirements. The meeting agenda primarily focuses on key risk and audit matters relevant to the CEO and each Group Executive’s performance and remuneration outcomes so that consideration is given to both exceptional and poor risk and audit outcomes and the context in which those outcomes occurred. The Group Risk & Remuneration Review Committee is a management committee that advises the Group CRO on risk considerations for determining remuneration outcomes. This Committee also reviews the application of remuneration consequences for poor risk behaviours and/or outcomes on accountable individuals from Executive Managers to Executive General Managers, including Specified Roles. In line with regulatory requirements, the performance and remuneration arrangements and outcomes of the CEO ASB are approved by the ASB Board and reported to the PRC with the request that the PRC recommend them to the CBA Board for approval, contingent on the ASB Board approval.

## **External advisors** During the 2025 financial year, external advisors were engaged to provide information to the People & Remuneration Committee to assist the Committee with making remuneration decisions. The People & Remuneration Committee did not seek or receive any remuneration recommendations from external advisors in the 2025 financial year.

## **Hedging policy** Employees are prohibited from hedging, or otherwise limiting, their economic exposure to equity price risk in relation to unvested equity-linked remuneration issued under any Group equity arrangement. CBA Board Directors, the CEO, Group Executives and their associates must not hedge their exposure to vested Group securities. Breaches of this requirement may result in disciplinary action, including the forfeiture and/or lapsing of unvested awards. Further details of hedging restrictions are set out in the Group Personal Trading Policy, previously called the Group Securities Trading Policy. The ASB Personal Trading Policy approved by the ASB Board sets out equivalent prohibitions against the hedging of Group securities by ASB Directors (including the ASB CEO) and ASB employees. **The Group Personal Trading Policy is available at commbank.com.au/corporategovernance** 214 215 Remuneration report (continued)

During the 2025 financial year, CBA’s consequence management processes identified 1,959 instances (FY24: 2,259) of substantiated misconduct, with 184 (FY24: 180) resulting in termination.

## Risk assessment in performance and remuneration **CBA’s performance and remuneration frameworks** support effective risk management by holding employees individually and collectively accountable for managing role-related risks, encouraging behaviour that aligns with the Group’s values, performance management framework, and Code of Conduct. Employees are also required to complete Group mandatory learning. **Group-wide risk assessment guidance** including examples is regularly reviewed to set clear expectations of managing risks for both employees and managers, and to help people leaders consistently assess risk behaviours and outcomes, determine the appropriate level of STVR adjustments for not fully meeting expectations, and document the reasons for their assessment. **ELT risk assessments** continue to be supported by executive risk scorecards, independent assessment by the Group CRO, and the Board Committees meet concurrently as part of the interim and annual performance assessment processes. **Comprehensive reporting** is provided to the Board to support its oversight of risk assessment and remuneration outcomes and to inform the Board’s guidance for the annual performance and remuneration review.

text: ## **Auditor independence** The operation of the Group External Auditor Services Policy assists in ensuring the independence of the Group’s external auditor. The Audit Committee has considered the provision, during the year, of non-audit services by PwC, and has concluded that the provision of those services did not compromise the auditor independence requirements of the _Corporations Act 2001_ (Cth). The Audit Committee is satisfied that the provision of the non-audit services by PwC during the year is compatible with the general standard of independence for auditors imposed by the _Corporations Act 2001_ (Cth). The Directors have considered the provision of non-audit services by PwC for the year ended 30 June 2025 and are satisfied that, in accordance with the advice received from the Board Audit Committee, such services are compatible with the general standard of independence for auditors and did not compromise the auditor independence requirements of the _Corporations Act 2001_ (Cth). The reasons for this are as follows: - the effective operation of the Group External Auditor Services Policy during the year to restrict the nature of non-audit services engagements, to prohibit certain services and to require Board Audit Committee pre-approval for all such engagements; and - the relative quantum of fees paid for non-audit services compared to the quantum for audit, and audit-related services was appropriate.
